{quote}If you have any optimization tips and tricks{quote}

Now how much time is forever 😄 As we are essentially recalculating full balance of all partners the compute takes quite a bit yes but try to use partition keys as much as possible & resources available in prod are much bigger compared your local cluster. So I don’t think it’s a huge blocker. 

Another idea is to calculate the current balance from beginning only once. And then next week we just calculate the weekly balance sum & then add it to the previous week’s current balance e.g.

* current balance today = 100 eur
* next weeks sum of all balance entries = -50 eur
* next week’s current balance = 100 - 50 = 50 eur

This way we don’t have to calculate full balance over & over again. Weekly interval is much more performant

# Legal view

Bolt should not impose any specific Economic Activity Code (CAE) on its fleet partners, considering that they are legally autonomous entities with full freedom of economic initiative. The choice of CAE(s) to be adopted in the course of their business activity is the sole responsibility of the partners themselves, in coordination with their accountants and tax advisors.

Bolt does not provide tax or accounting advice and, as such, does not condition the provision of services on the adoption of any particular CAE.

# Non binding information (for external reference, if requested)

Without prejudice to the above position, and solely for informational purposes, the CAEs most commonly associated with food delivery activities in the digital platform sector are, in fact:

* *53200* – Other postal and courier activities
* *53201* – Courier services
* *53202* – Other postal and courier activities, except those carried out by CTT (national postal service)

These CAEs are compatible with the general description of home delivery services.

The CAEs currently referenced (e.g. 1519 – Other food manufacturing industries and 64120 – Other monetary intermediation) do not reflect the typical activity of food delivery operations and may be inappropriate for practical purposes. However, the decision to retain or remove them lies solely with the partner and should be assessed within the context of their business model.

An archive job is often stuck in a specific Execution State, as illustrated in the following example: 1. It enters the READER_IN state and retrieves the objects. 2. The archiver encounters issues and breaks down for various reasons. 3. The archiver then restarts and begins again from the READER_IN state, repeating this cycle. One potential solution would be to modify the ArchiveJobFsm to detect consecutive occurrences of the same Execution State. For instance, if there are 10 consecutive states, we should notify the owners that their archiver may be stuck. Additionally, we could attach an error message to display in the user interface.

Hello Team!

I completely understand why this might look like a double charge, but I can assure you that the user was only charged once. This is a common part of how card payments are processed. Here's what happens:

# When the user first makes a payment, the bank temporarily ‘reserves' the funds and this is just the bank setting aside the amount for the transaction. The user’s account balance might show less amount but the payment hasn’t actually been taken out by the bank yet.
# Later, when the payment is fully processed, that reserved amount is now “officially” debited from the user’s account. At that point, some banks send a second notification, which can make it seem like a second charge.


I would advise the user to check their final account balance or statement, where they can confirm that only one payment was actually withdrawn. The earlier “pending” amount will either drop off or convert into the final charge.

Cheers,
Afiba

Hi [~accountid:712020:bc7bca9c-4d13-42b6-9684-04014a47f7aa] , I’ve aligned with Central Legal on this one as the situation is rather peculiar. Please see some guidance below - which has been checked against our DK T&Cs (for Bolt, not 4x27): 

*Our obligations and choices*

* Bolt’s obligations depend on any transport regulatory duties that apply to it by law. Where such duties exist, Bolt must comply. *Outside those cases, it is not Bolt’s role to intervene in the relationship between fleet owners and drivers*.
* That said, Bolt may still choose to investigate suspected breaches of its terms (see section 9 of our T&Cs). Fleets remain responsible for preventing unlawful behaviour on the platform (section 9.1) and must not allow conduct that could significantly harm Bolt’s reputation (section 5.6.1.2.3). Bolt may suspend or terminate a fleet driver’s access - as part of the fleet’s overall access - where breaches occur (sections 10 and 11). *This enables Bolt to address problematic fleet drivers.*
* A fleet’s claim that a driver is “bad” is *not*, +on its own+, *a valid reason to refuse re-registration*. Bolt should be able to verify any problems independently, not rely on hearsay, if it's going to restrict access and prevent 're-registrations' with another fleet.

*Re-registering*

* Bolt reserves the right to refuse platform access to any fleet driver who has previously caused a fleet to be in breach of the terms (see section 7.4). The licence for a driver to access the platform continues only while there is no risk of damage to Bolt’s reputation (section 5.6.1.2.3). These provisions give Bolt sufficient discretion to prevent problem drivers from returning to the platform... *assuming there is a documented ground for suspension that we can rely on for these purposes*.
* In practice, details of any problem driver should be recorded so onboarding can be blocked if they attempt to re-register. The safety team likely already manages this for removed drivers. If not, that process +should+ be established.

*Next steps and other considerations*

* If we want to take action, we need to find a breach of our terms that we will rely on to suspend access.
* If the local ops team want to prevent re-registrations, the team should involve the safety team to identify how to stop that individual rejoining the platform. There should already be a process or flagging mechanism for this.
* Depending on licensing rules, the fleet (or Bolt) could also consider reporting the driver to the relevant regulatory body. Bolt can choose to do so as well, but any concerns should be well substantiated.
* *Could you please confirm whether this situation involves a 4x27 driver*? If so, we need to do the equivalent check of the the 4x27 T&Cs - as the above advice relates to our own T&Cs [here|https://bolt.eu/en-dk/legal/platform-terms-for-ride-hailing-services-service-providers-denmark/?category=rides].

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Afiba

Hello,

The customer used an APM (Alternative Payment Method) to place the order and this type of payment methods does not have a preauthorisation option that is later reversed. They only support a direct charge on the card. So if the user makes an order but then cancels it, in this case we refund their money unlike preauthorisation where we just release the reserved amount. 
So in this case, the user placed an order and we charged them higher, but at the end of the ride, the order price decreased or the order is cancelled, so automatically we refunded them the difference. But later on from your end (CS) you initiated a full refund, which was applied to the first higher order amount. And this is what creates the debt as the balance thinks that we have returned the full amount to the user, meaning whatever the user previously paid was all returned to them. But since a service was provided to the user for the order or cancellation fee, it is still trying to charge the user for the extra refunded amount. That is where the debt comes from.

Could you complete a refund to the user’s balance on a different order to compensate for the debt in their account?

I have reviewed and marked up both influencer agreements (Raimonds Stutans’ and Matthew McElhinney’s) to address the key legal and operational risks identified (please see mark-ups linked at the bottom). To summarise, the following material updates have been made in the main contract terms:

* *Termination Rights*
** Made asymmetric – Bolt can terminate on notice; Talent only for cause.
* *Licence & Image Rights*
** Replaced perpetual, exclusive licence with a non-exclusive, 2-year licence.
** Added explicit moral rights waiver under the UK Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988.
* *Morality Clause*
** Added express right for Bolt to terminate immediately for reputational harm or inappropriate conduct.
* *Advertising Compliance*
** Added reference to UK CAP Code and ASA guidance on influencer marketing.
* *Data Protection (Clause 11)*
** Updated to reflect UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018.
** Named the ICO as the UK supervisory authority and referenced the UK Addendum to SCCs for any overseas transfers.
* *Payment Trigger*
** Added condition precedent that payment is only due after Bolt’s written approval of all deliverables; no invoice permitted until approval.
* *Audit / Proof of Posting*
** Added clause giving Bolt the right to request proof of posting and requiring posts to remain live for 60 days after the campaign.

These updates align the agreements with UK advertising, data-protection, and contract-law standards.

----

h3. *2️⃣ Points Still Requiring Business Input (SOW Updates Needed)*

The following items must be clarified or corrected directly in the Statement of Work (SOW) for each influencer by the business.

----

*Ambiguous Deliverables / Posting Details*

* *Why this matters:* Lack of detail on posting frequency, hashtags, captions, and approval timelines risks poor-quality or late content.
* *What needs to be done:* Add a specific posting schedule, required hashtags/captions, and approval turnaround (e.g. “Bolt to review within 3 business days”).

----

*Date Mismatch Between Agreement and SOW*

* *Why this matters:* Matthew’s SOW is dated December 2024 but the main agreement is dated November 2025 and refers to a campaign running from 6 Nov 2025 to 28 Feb 2025, creating inconsistent or impossible campaign dates. Raimonds’ SOW is also dated December 2024 but the main agreement is dated November 2025 and there is no campaign end date.
* *What needs to be done:* Align SOW dates with the main agreement (same year, correct campaign period).

----

*Ambiguous “Organic Content is Indefinite” in SOW*

* *Why this matters:* SOW (item 5) grants indefinite organic usage rights but paid advertising licence is undefined (“License Length for paid advertising” with no duration stated). Missing duration for paid ads creates ambiguity; influencer could claim perpetual paid use was not agreed or was limited. Potential IP dispute or ASA complaint for continuing to use content after campaign ends.
*What needs to be done:* Define clear time limits for both organic and paid-media use (e.g. 12 or 24 months).

----

*Exclusivity / Territory Confusion*

* *Why this matters:* The “Territory” section lists “7 TikTok posts” and mixes geography with deliverables.
* *What needs to be done:* Separate and clarify Deliverables, Exclusivity, and Territory fields. Confirm actual posting requirements.

----

*Fee / Tax Treatment*

* *Why this matters:* Ambiguity on VAT and tax obligations could create HMRC risk.
* *What needs to be done:* State explicitly that the fee is inclusive of VAT (if applicable) and that the influencer is responsible for self-assessment taxes.

----

*Approval of Blog Content*

* *Why this matters:* The SOW requires one blog but doesn’t specify hosting site or approval process.
* *What needs to be done:* Specify platform (e.g. Bolt blog or influencer’s own site) and require Bolt’s pre-approval before publication.

----

*Misalignment of Deliverables Across Platforms*

* *Why this matters:* Conflicting numbers (e.g. in Matthew’s SOW there is 2 TikToks 2 IG, 2 Facebook, 1 blog, vs 7 TikToks) create uncertainty about deliverables.
* *What needs to be done:* Consolidate deliverables into a single list or table showing the exact number per platform.

----

*No Performance Milestones*

* *Why this matters:* There is no timeline or breach trigger if posts are delayed or incomplete.
* *What needs to be done:* Add clear deadlines and approval milestones for each deliverable.

----

h3. *3️⃣ Next Steps for the Business*

# Return the revised SOWs for final legal review before circulation to the influencers for signature.

As such, we can {color:#36b37e}*proceed*{color} with this from the privacy side ✅ , +*_provided that_*+ the following mitigations are adopted:

{panel:bgColor=#eae6ff}
* *Disabling marketing consents*: For passengers using the kiosk that have not previously owned a Bolt account, I understand that a form of profile will be automatically created for them when they order a trip. Any marketing / promotional consents on this profile should be disabled by default.
* *Kiosk provider data sharing*: As part of the contract we are negotiating with the kiosk provider, we should include a data sharing agreement to ensure that any personal data being exchanged is protected. {color:#4c9aff}*Please loop me in when we are at the contract negotiation stage*{color}, and I can prepare this DSA.
* *Disclaimer language*: To meet transparency requirements under UA law, we should do the following:
** (1) Ensure that a link to the correct (UA) passenger privacy notice is available at relevant stages of the order flow. In particular:
*** (i) When making the order via the touchscreen -> Include: “_By booking, you agree with Bolt’s terms and acknowledge Bolt’s privacy notice available at [HYPERLINK]”_
*** (ii) On printed ride receipts for passengers → Include: “_Bolt processes your personal data in accordance with its privacy notice: [FULL TEXT HYPERLINK]_”. This hyperlink should be full text so that the passenger can separately type it int a computer.
** (2) Ensure that during the order flow, both Bolt’s and the kiosk provider’s company name and registered address are visible somewhere (e.g., in small text at the bottom of the screen). It appears that this is a requirement under local law.
* *Receipt contents*: We should ensure that QR codes available on rides receipts only work for a limited period of time (so that not just anyone with access to the code can access the receipt). We should also ensure that we are only including driver and passenger information on the receipt that is strictly necessary. Finally, we should ensure that the passenger is provided with a booking reference number which, when provided to Bolt CS, allows CS to identify the relevant trip and assist with any passenger queries/complaints.
* *Touchscreen auto-clearance*: If a passenger starts to put their details into the order flow, but does not complete it, we should ensure that such information is not retained by either the kiosk provider nor Bolt.

*Ticket RS-1860 – Ukraine*

*Authority:* Main Department of the National Police in Kharkiv Region, Police Department No. 2
*Date:* 31 October 2025
*Case No.:* 12025226260000237
*Legal basis cited:* Article 162 of the _Criminal Procedure Code of Ukraine_ (CPC)
*Purpose:* Pre-trial investigation under Article 190(1) of the _Criminal Code of Ukraine_ (fraud).
*Data requested:*

* Addresses to which taxi orders were made from 19 August 2025 to the present;
* Paid using card account No. 5472761255057338 (registered to _Fursov Oleksandr Oleksandrovych_);
* Potentially associated with phone number +380997630677.

----

h3. 1. Legal basis assessment

According to Bolt’s accepted legal bases list for *Ukraine*, valid disclosure can occur only under:

* _Criminal Procedure Code of Ukraine_, *Articles 93 and 159–164* — i.e. data requests backed by a *court order* for temporary access to documents or things.

The police here cite *Article 162 CPC*, which only _defines_ information protected by law (e.g. correspondence, personal data, financial info) and regulates conditions of access. It does *not grant police direct power to obtain data from private entities* without a court order.

Hence, *Article 162 CPC alone is not a valid or enforceable legal basis* for disclosure.

----

h3. 2. Scope and proportionality

The police request *all ride addresses* from 19 August 2025 to present — a time span of several months — even though the alleged fraudulent payment occurred on 19 August 2025.
This is disproportionate: only data around the transaction date (e.g. ±3 days) could be relevant to the case.

----

h3. 3. Decision

*→ Deny disclosure; request clarification.*

Bolt cannot share any data based solely on Article 162 CPC.
Disclosure requires a *court order under Articles 159–164 CPC* specifying the data scope, timeframe, and the reason the data are relevant to the investigation.

----

h3. *Summary*

Police in Kharkiv requested ride address data linked to a bank card used in an alleged fraud. They relied on Article 162 CPC, which is not a valid legal basis for disclosure without a court order. Request is also excessive in scope.
*Action:* Decline disclosure; instruct CS to request a proper court order and limit the timeframe.

----

*On the requested data:*

The connection between the requested data and the alleged fraud is very weak.

The facts show a classic *online purchase scam*: money was transferred from the victim’s bank card to another individual’s card (Fursov’s), supposedly for a pair of shoes. The police discovered that this recipient’s card was later used to pay for Bolt rides, and they now want the *addresses of those rides*.

However, *ride destination data does not meaningfully prove or disprove* whether the cardholder (or another person using the card) committed fraud. At most, it might show where the user travelled — but that’s not directly relevant to establishing the identity of the fraudster or the path of the stolen funds. Bolt is not a financial intermediary in the transfer; we merely processed payments for trips.

So in GDPR terms, the request *fails the necessity and proportionality test*:

* *Necessity:* The rides’ addresses are not necessary to trace the alleged fraudulent transaction. The relevant financial information (timestamps, payment identifiers) should be obtained from the bank, not Bolt.
* *Proportionality:* Even if the police were investigating whether Fursov exists or is active in Kharkiv, that could be done with far less intrusive data (e.g. account registration details or confirmation of activity).

Unless the police can show that the Bolt rides themselves were part of the fraud (e.g. used to transport goods purchased with stolen money), sharing ride addresses would expose location data unrelated to the alleged offence — clearly disproportionate.

In short: *the request doesn’t logically support the investigation purpose*. That reinforces the conclusion to deny disclosure and ask the police to justify why these data points are relevant, alongside providing a valid legal basis.

Hey [~accountid:712020:9cfda827-f644-48a1-9da8-aff3fd427bf9] !

[~accountid:712020:705c56b5-c931-428e-8282-8c20af89d9c2] asked us a similar question and our advise at the time was that _“Our view is that couriers shouldn't sign up directly on our platform, but we can have and display a list of ‘active’ fleets that have authorised Bolt to share their contact details to couriers.”_

While we understand your question is a bit different (couriers to manifest their intention to work w/ us directly on our website instead of signing up directly in our Platform), we believe the proposal presented is still problematic, for the following reasons:

* The act of “manifesting intention to work with Bolt” directly on our site — even if followed by referral to a fleet — creates a documented link between Bolt and the courier, which can be interpreted as an employment-style pre-contractual relationship.
* Data capture + redirection can look like Bolt is screening or initiating the onboarding, and the fleet is simply executing — which undermines the fleet’s independent role.
* This adds weight to reclassification arguments, especially in inspections or disputes.

Therefore, from a legal standpoint, we’d advise *not collecting courier information directly via our website*, even if the goal is just to pass it to fleets. Allowing couriers to submit their interest to “work with Bolt” — and then redirecting them — could still create the perception that *Bolt is actively sourcing or screening couriers*, which may *blur the legal separation* between Bolt and the couriers and increase *reclassification risk*.

Instead, an alternative and safer approach would be to:

* *List active fleet partners (with their consent)* on our site, organized by geo;
* Include their *contact info or link to their sign-up forms*;
* Let couriers *reach out directly* to the fleet of their choice.

We’re happy to support on framing or reviewing the copy for such a page. 

Thank you!

** Added reference to UK CAP Code and ASA guidance on influencer marketing.

** Added condition precedent that payment is only due after Bolt’s written approval of all deliverables; no invoice permitted until approval.
* *Audit / Proof of Posting*
** Added clause giving Bolt the right to request proof of posting and requiring posts to remain live for 60 days after the campaign.

These updates align the agreements with UK advertising, data-protection, and contract-law standards.

----

h3. *2️⃣ Points Still Requiring Business Input (SOW Updates Needed)*

The following items must be clarified or corrected directly in the Statement of Work (SOW) for each influencer by the business.

----

*Ambiguous Deliverables / Posting Details*

* *Why this matters:* Lack of detail on posting frequency, hashtags, captions, and approval timelines risks poor-quality or late content.
* *What needs to be done:* Add a specific posting schedule, required hashtags/captions, and approval turnaround (e.g. “Bolt to review within 3 business days”).

----

*Date Mismatch Between Agreement and SOW*

* *Why this matters:* Matthew’s SOW is dated December 2024 but the main agreement is dated November 2025 and refers to a campaign running from 6 Nov 2025 to 28 Feb 2025, creating inconsistent or impossible campaign dates. Raimonds’ SOW is also dated December 2024 but the main agreement is dated November 2025 and there is no campaign end date.
* *What needs to be done:* Align SOW dates with the main agreement (same year, correct campaign period).

----

*Ambiguous “Organic Content is Indefinite” in SOW*

* *Why this matters:* SOW (item 5) grants indefinite organic usage rights but paid advertising licence is undefined (“License Length for paid advertising” with no duration stated). Missing duration for paid ads creates ambiguity; influencer could claim perpetual paid use was not agreed or was limited. Potential IP dispute or ASA complaint for continuing to use content after campaign ends.
*What needs to be done:* Define clear time limits for both organic and paid-media use (e.g. 12 or 24 months).

----

*Exclusivity / Territory Confusion*

* *Why this matters:* The “Territory” section lists “7 TikTok posts” and mixes geography with deliverables.
* *What needs to be done:* Separate and clarify Deliverables, Exclusivity, and Territory fields. Confirm actual posting requirements.

----

*Fee / Tax Treatment*

* *Why this matters:* Ambiguity on VAT and tax obligations could create HMRC risk.
* *What needs to be done:* State explicitly that the fee is inclusive of VAT (if applicable) and that the influencer is responsible for self-assessment taxes.

----

*Approval of Blog Content*

* *Why this matters:* The SOW requires one blog but doesn’t specify hosting site or approval process.
* *What needs to be done:* Specify platform (e.g. Bolt blog or influencer’s own site) and require Bolt’s pre-approval before publication.

----

*Misalignment of Deliverables Across Platforms*

* *Why this matters:* Conflicting numbers (e.g. in Matthew’s SOW there is 2 TikToks 2 IG, 2 Facebook, 1 blog, vs 7 TikToks) create uncertainty about deliverables.
* *What needs to be done:* Consolidate deliverables into a single list or table showing the exact number per platform.

----

*No Performance Milestones*

* *Why this matters:* There is no timeline or breach trigger if posts are delayed or incomplete.
* *What needs to be done:* Add clear deadlines and approval milestones for each deliverable.

----

h3. *3️⃣ Next Steps for the Business*

** Payment already visible in Admin Panel or posted while waiting.
** Recent payments (< 48 h) → template response used.
** Customer only wanted confirmation.
* *Tier 2 escalations (≈ 65 %)*:
** Payment not visible after 48 h.
** Missing / partial payment reference or multiple transactions to reconcile.
** Account still blocked even after payment.
** Complex SD involvement (manual posting, cross-invoice issues).

✅ *Takeaway:* Escalation frequency and dependency on Tier 2/SD are high, creating extended resolution times and queueing.

hi [~accountid:712020:f1fcbe05-e4af-4cd0-b974-656802946f17] Croatian regulations distinguish only between (1) taxi transport and (2) regular passenger (bus or coach) services. Your model that uses fixed route, fixed timetable, shared rides,  sits between the two. Because there is no legal definition of microtransit, regulators may interpret it as either a taxi or a regular passenger service.

To avoid the higher licensing requirements that apply to bus or coach services, the pilot should be framed and operated as an experimental extension of taxi services, using already licensed taxi drivers and vehicles.

*What needs to be done*

# Use only vehicles and drivers holding valid taxi licences issued by the City of Zagreb.
# Keep the pilot clearly limited in time and scale, for example, 5–7 days and a small number of routes.
# I would suggest informing the City of Zagreb’s transport department before launch, explaining it is a short pilot under existing taxi authorisations. - to be discussed with Public Policy - [~accountid:63314e9e9b32cfef93265252] 
# Avoid marketing language that suggests a scheduled or public transport service. Describe it as a “shared ride pilot” operated through licensed taxis.
# Confirm that all pickup and drop-off points are in legal taxi or parking zones approved for commercial use. [~accountid:63314e9e9b32cfef93265252] 

*Main risks*

*Reclassification risk:* The city or ministry could classify the service as “regular passenger transport,” which would require a national licence. This can be mitigated by keeping the pilot small, limiting its duration, and aligning it with the existing taxi framework.

*Local enforcement risk:* Depending on the local rules - city inspectors could issue fines if routes or pickup points are not compliant with local rules. This risk can be reduced through prior engagement with city authorities and by using only authorised taxi stands.

*Insurance risk:* If the service were viewed as a bus-type operation, existing insurance might not apply. 

*Future licensing risk:* Any wider or longer-term rollout would likely require a new licence or a change in the regulatory framework. The pilot should therefore focus on collecting data to support future regulatory discussions.



The pilot can proceed under existing taxi licences as a controlled, short-term test, provided it remains limited, transparent, and compliant with Zagreb’s taxi rules. 

If the regulator later decides the model qualifies as “regular passenger transport,” a national passenger transport licence could be required for any future expansion.

Hi [~accountid:712020:dbc22d70-1983-4414-80b3-27f087787ae4] 

Following the inquiry from the Estonian Consumer Protection Authority (TTJA) regarding the Paris ride paid in cash, and their position that Bolt is obliged to refund the rider via cash or bank transfer (as opposed to a promo code), here’s our legal position.

h2. Legal Assessment

# No express legal obligation to refund in cash or bank transfer

Under both EU and French consumer law, particularly Directive 2011/83/EU (Article 13), the trader is required to issue a refund “using the same means of payment used by the consumer,” _unless the consumer agrees otherwise_. However, this obligation applies where the trader originally received the payment.

In this case, the cash payment was made directly to the driver. Bolt never received these funds and therefore:

* Did not process the transaction itself;
* Is not, strictly speaking, reimbursing a payment it received.

Under French transport law (Article L.3142-3 of the Transport Code), Bolt remains contractually liable for service performance but not for managing the funds in cash transactions. Offering a promo code of equal value is a recognized way to remedy a service failure, provided it doesn’t impose undue burden on the consumer.

h2. 2. Offering a promo code is legally defensible

Promo codes are generally considered an acceptable form of redress _if_:

* They match the value of the failed service,
* They are valid for a reasonable time,
* They can be used easily in the same context (i.e., the Bolt app).

These criteria align with consumer protection goals: restoring the customer’s ability to access the paid-for service, rather than insisting on form over function.

Of course, if we want to avoid any legal dispute, we may want to refund through another means.

Thanks,

Elisabetta

*Answers:*

After reviewing the Special Terms we have agreed with the partner [+HERE+|https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1I29rG7d1D_9l27Y6kzP9VTlt9KjRx9Sl] it is clear that:

# *It was agreed on Special Terms, that Special Terms itself can be changed only mutually if both parties agree to it* - cls 7 at the [+end of the page+|https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1I29rG7d1D_9l27Y6kzP9VTlt9KjRx9Sl]. It is NOT however mentioned, that Bolt cannot change general T&Cs and its terms which are NOT regulated under the Special Terms separately.
## *This means, that all* +*other*+ *terms* [+*under the general T&Cs*+|https://bolt.eu/lv-lv/legal/tnc-partners/?category=delivery] (i.e. the ones always publicly available on Bolt’s legal webpage and updated from time to time) *can be changed unilaterally by Bolt at any time, by giving a prior 30 day notice to the partner*.  If partner do not object the T&Cs change by e.g. terminating the agreement or negotiating new terms for themselves under the Special Terms, then it is considered that partner has accepted updated general T&Cs +to the extent that they don’t contradict the terms that was separately agreed under the Special Terms document+.
## The general T&Cs which we have currently up were uploaded on 26.08.2025 and respective email was sent out to all partners contact emails on 29.08 stating clearly that new terms will be applicable 30 days after receiving this email, unless they object those. Currently it seems that this partner has not objected those within this 30 days after receiving the email. Unless you have received respective email +before+ 30.09.  *Hence,* [+*general T&Cs available*+|https://bolt.eu/lv-lv/legal/tnc-partners/?category=delivery] *on our homepage currently apply to them to the extent they don’t* [+*contradict Special Terms*+|https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1I29rG7d1D_9l27Y6kzP9VTlt9KjRx9Sl]*.* For example - definitions, intellectual property rights, etc are explicitly agreed on under the Special Terms document, which means that those terms remain +as they are+.
# *Regarding privacy part,* then parties agreed on it separately under the Special Terms - page 9, Schedule 2 changes as Tatsiana also mentioned. +This means that unless Parties agree mutually in writing otherwise, then new privacy terms which are valid currently, won’t apply to the partner+. As Tatsiana confirmed, then for privacy team it is okey to keep the “old” regulation what was agreed on back in 2020. Meaning, for the partner nothing should change from the privacy side.

+*UPDATE - NETHERLANDS (12.11)*+

* Legal SD ticket is here ([+LSS-47515+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-47515]). Created in June 2025. Unsurprisingly, Privacy Team was not looped in.
** It appears that the roll-out is part of a tender application at Schiphol airport (see [here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/15rXHxPNyD9e3sA4-rtMccCT-yfhNlPXAdwhbETtaaUU/edit?tab=t.0]). In which case, the launch itself is permissible.
** Involves a partnership with Taxicoach (fleet operator, 75 vehicles in operation, all must be Bolt branded). Taxicoach would manage supply through a fleet account.
** Bolt has partnered with Noot and Mobilitas (tender agreement is [here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1yjA3YiiyGL4vCEATPPbvgXVpsG0RBLH1IzVwmNVYME4/edit?tab=t.0]).
*** Noot submitted tender application. Bolt provides platform. Mobilitas is operations handler.
*** At first glance, it does not appear that any third-party integrations are happening here. Rather, fleet drivers will effectively be using part of the Bolt app to take trips.
*** 45 vehicles operating in the airport. 30 operating in Amsterdam.
*** No obvious data sharing provisions.
* We otherwise do not have visibility of the specifics of the rolled-out feature itself.

+*THOUGHTS*+

* GDPR applies, so I can nudge the following usual advice:
** Passenger should have a booking reference number.
** There should be some form of location control here - either switching off the feature of keeping the fleet itself location-restricted.
** Safety features relying on passenger consent should not be enabled by default.
** Limited transparency language should be provided via the QR code.
** Invoices should not contain any unnecessary user data.
* In terms of data sharing, it is unclear if Bolt is sharing personal data with Noot and Mobilitas.
** If Bolt is, then we should get an agreement in place. If not, then we can decide to proceed without a DSA, as technically there are no third-party integrations  the fleet driver is the one sharing the data.
* I have messaged on the thread [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C080LNBM05A/p1762943246561739?thread_ts=1762876555.389819&cid=C080LNBM05A].

We’re seeing a race condition due to the order of the order_courier rows. When the same courier is dispatched to the same order multiple times, we first remove the order from the cached active orders for the given courier, and then we add it back. This relies on the order of the order_courier rows, which in some cases could be unexpected.

We’re sorting by last_update, created. As we see in the example below, the previous assignment was last updated after the creation of the new assignment, which most likely switched the order of the cache commands at that time, resulting in adding the active order, and then removing it. That way the courier didn’t see the order as active.

When we’re adding a new order_courier, we update the previous one to link the new one through {{retry_to_order_courier_id}}. Because the insert and the update are separate statements, while in the same transaction, the current timestamp is not guaranteed to be the same, hence the issue, as the update is done after the insert.

Hey [~accountid:712020:9cfda827-f644-48a1-9da8-aff3fd427bf9] !

On the idea of shortlisting fleets based on Bolt’s own criteria, we’d flag a few concerns from a legal and compliance standpoint:

* *Competition & fairness:* If Bolt selects which fleets appear on a public list, and this results in some fleets receiving more visibility or access to courier leads, it may be seen as favoring certain partners over others. This could raise concerns under competition law principles, especially if the selection criteria are not transparent or objectively applied.
* *Platform neutrality (P2B Regulation):* As a platform, we’re expected to treat business users (e.g. fleets) fairly and transparently. If we promote some but not others — without a clear, objective basis — it could be perceived as discriminatory or non-neutral.
* *Reputational risk:* Excluded fleets may raise fairness complaints, which could erode trust and potentially attract scrutiny if challenged.

To mitigate this, we’d suggest an *opt-in model* where:

* Any fleet that is operational in a given geo, currently onboarding couriers, and agrees *not to charge onboarding fees* can be listed;
* Bolt publishes *transparent and objective participation criteria*, applied equally;
* The page uses neutral language — e.g. “participating fleets” — and avoids value judgments like “preferred” or “recommended”.

As for *lead tracking:* as mentioned earlier, Bolt should not collect or manage courier intent or contact tracking, as this reintroduces reclassification risks and blurs legal lines. 

Thank you!

In our view, there are no major legal blockers to the “Day in the Life of a Courier” initiative, provided the following conditions are met:
– Participation is voluntary and clearly framed as a team-building/awareness activity.
– A consent form is signed by each participant, clarifying risks, safety rules, and personal responsibility for any traffic violations.
– All participants receive a safety briefing and suitable equipment.

I recommend a short *consent + safety form*, and run the activity in line with Bolt's OHS policies.

I would also advise you to consult People Partner ([~accountid:712020:c6aafe58-3b3b-42c5-b22d-76a1d553b53c] ) to: 

* Make sure that the company ensures proper *insurance coverage*, including liability if employees use bicycles or vehicles on public roads.
* Define at which hours this would be done (working hours Vs extra), necessity of managers approval in case it is in working hours, etc.

Thank you!

Hey team,

Legal decided to externalize this, since, as mentioned in our comment, the information provided was based on online information.

External counsel comments are the following: 

+*On Online Sales and Internet Pharmacies:*+

*Fenech + Fenech Comments:*

_We are not fully aligned with the assessment made above. It is not so clear, under the overarching regulatory framework, that licenced physical pharmacies can use digital platforms and couriers to fulfil orders for medicinal products without approval from the Superintendent for Public Health for the below reasons:_

# _The Medicines Act defines:_

* _“_*_dispensing_*_” as the sale or supply of medicinal products from a pharmacy;_
* _"_*_good practice_*_" in relation to manufacturing practice, laboratory practice, distribution practice, clinical practice and dispensing practice means the standards for the proper execution of the relative activity as established by or under this Act;_
* +_Article 76. (1) of the Medicines Act: Unless otherwise provided by or under this Act, a medicinal product_+ +*_shall only be prepared or dispensed from a pharmacy and by a pharmacist._*+ 

# _We are of the opinion that the relevant authorities interpret this definition very restrictively and would interpret the act of “dispensing”. We are also aware that the only active delivery schemes in Malta, the POYC scheme which delivers free medicine to eligible patients and other community pharmacies, are in fact carried out by pharmacists themselves and would have obtained specific clearance from the Superintendent from Public Health._ 
# _The Malta Medicine’s Authority website states: The Malta Medicines Authority regulates pharmacy practice activities including deliveries of medicinal products from licensed pharmacies. It then goes on to link to the Pharmacy Council Directive:_ *_Directive for Digital Activity dated 4th June 2020 (attached)._*
# _The_ *_directive_* _provides that:_

_a) Digital site: For the intents and purposes of this document, the term digital site shall be taken to mean a Website. It is to be made clear that all other forms of digital media platforms, including mobile apps, are excluded from this definition. The use of such digital media platforms is prohibited._ 

_The digital site must not be promoted through search engine optimisers or similar services and must also not be advertised or promoted in any way._

_In view of the regulatory lack of clarity and our experience with the Malta Medicines Authority and the Superintendent of Public Health we are of the opinion that they will take an extremely restrictive view and interpretation of the applicable laws._ 

+*On “A. OTC (Non-Prescription) Medicines”:*+

*Fenech + Fenech Comments:*

_The assessment’s analysis of OTC medicine sales and delivery is premised on the assumption that licensed pharmacies may lawfully use third-party digital platforms and couriers (such as Bolt) to facilitate the sale and delivery of medicines. However, since Maltese law does not expressly permit or regulate the use of such third-party intermediaries for medicine delivery, any conclusions regarding the lawfulness of online sales, platform requirements, or delivery logistics for OTC medicines are uncertain and speculative at this stage._



+*On “B. Prescription Medicines”:*+

*Fenech + Fenech Comments:*

_The requirements for prescription validation, pharmacist oversight, and secure handling are all discussed in the context of a delivery model involving third-party platforms and couriers. The assessment’s recommendations on prescription upload, pharmacist checks, and courier handover cannot be validated since the legal uncertainty about the permissibility of third-party involvement means that the entire framework for prescription medicine delivery described in the assessment may not be compliant with Maltese law, regardless of the safeguards proposed._


+*On Conditions for Lawful Courier Delivery:*+

*Fenech + Fenech Comments:*

_This section outlines the conditions under which courier delivery would be lawful, assuming that such a model is permitted. However, in view of the fact that the law and the Malta Medicine’s Authority position is ambiguous on whether third-party couriers can be used at all, then specifying conditions for lawful delivery is premature._

_Without a clear legal basis for third-party courier involvement, it is not possible to confirm whether any set of operational conditions would render such deliveries lawful under Maltese law without at least obtaining a clarification on a no-names basis._ 



In light of external counsel’s opinion, the legal and regulatory framework in Malta regarding the use of third-party digital platforms and couriers for the sale and delivery of both OTC and prescription medicines remains *uncertain and highly restrictive*.

Given the shared advise, we *cannot confirm the legality of a courier-based delivery model* involving Bolt at this stage, even for OTC medicines.

As a result, w*e recommend that no operational steps are taken to onboard or service pharmacy clients in Malta unless and until formal clarification is obtained from the relevant authorities.*

We will continue to monitor developments and will coordinate with external counsel to explore next steps should the regulatory position evolve.

Hi Team,

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Afiba

Hi Team,

All these trips have a preauthorisation charge which can mislead the customer to think they were charged twice.
I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Afiba

Hi [~accountid:63b59fb7d3aeefa40543d2e5] have submitted the POA for signature. 

I know you mentioned legal review wasn’t needed, but given the importance of the airports and some of the terms in the agreement, I had a look and felt obliged to flag a few high-risk areas.

I've summarised them briefly for your review — ultimately it’s a commercial risk call, but these points stood out as significant. Do you think there’s any chance of success in requesting a few targeted amendments, just to help cap Bolt’s risk and bring the terms closer to our standard approach?

* *Exclusive Risk and Indemnity Burden*
{color:#ff5630}Clause 15{color} imposes a broad, one-sided indemnity on Bolt, covering all third-party claims — even those not caused by Bolt’s fault. There’s no reciprocal protection from FAAN. This creates significant exposure to uninsurable liabilities, especially in a public-regulated setting. Ideally, we’d seek to limit this to direct losses and introduce reciprocal obligations in line with Bolt’s standard terms.
* *No Data Protection or Confidentiality Clauses* - The agreement also gives FAAN broad audit and data access rights {color:#ff5630}(Clauses 4 and 7){color} with no limitations or safeguards, and it doesn’t include any confidentiality or data protection provisions at all. Given the potential access to driver, customer, and platform data, these gaps raise serious privacy and compliance concerns, and I believe they’ll need to be flagged with the [Privacy team for further review|https://taxify.atlassian.net/servicedesk/customer/portal/47/group/157/create/2105].
* *Termination for Breach – Clause 12(ii):*
This clause allows the Authority to terminate the agreement for *_any_* breach by Bolt with as little as 7 days’ notice, {color:#ff5630}regardless of severity or whether the breach has a material impact{color}. There’s no requirement for multiple or repeated breaches, no distinction between minor and serious failures, and no express obligation for the Authority to act reasonably or proportionately. This {color:#ff5630}creates a risk of immediate contract loss for issues that may be operationally routine or easily remediable{color}.
* *Broad and Subjective Performance Obligations – Clause 4:*
Numerous obligations are imposed across {color:#ff5630}sub-clauses 4(ix), (xii), (xvii), (xix), (xx), and (xxi){color} covering matters like system integration, vehicle and driver compliance, uptime targets, data sharing, and service availability. These obligations are not paired with defined SLAs, performance thresholds, or grace periods. In the absence of any qualifying language or remedy periods, any perceived non-compliance with these terms could technically constitute a breach and trigger termination under Clause 12(ii). {color:#ff5630}This structure exposes Bolt to a disproportionate risk of termination for operational variances or isolated driver conduct without opportunity to cure{color}.
* *Unilateral Audit Rights – Clause 4(xix):*
The Authority is granted unrestricted rights to audit Bolt’s operational records and usage data at any time, {color:#ff5630}without any notice requirements, scope limitations, or confidentiality obligations.{color} There are no safeguards to prevent misuse, overreach, or access to sensitive commercial or personal data beyond what is reasonably required. It is not unreasonable to request to include clear audit protocols, including minimum notice periods, defined scope and frequency, confidentiality protections for any data accessed, and a limitation to data strictly necessary for compliance purposes.

Hi Jasmina,

I've reviewed the proposed lottery structure and, from a legal standpoint (particularly under French labour law),I have reclassification concerns due to the way the reward is currently linked to driver performance on the Bolt app.

*Legal Risk in the Current Proposal*

The current setup — requiring 4 rides and 15 hours of weekly app connection to qualify — may appear modest, but it introduces performance-based eligibility criteria for receiving a benefit. This could be interpreted by a court as Bolt:

* *Controlling the driver’s activity (via thresholds and monitoring),*
* *Rewarding use of the Bolt platform rather than participation in a separate advertising service,*
* *And thus, creating an indirect exclusivity or dependency that weakens the independence of the driver.*

When combined with a substantial reward (€9,000), this starts to look more like a structured bonus scheme than a pure advertising incentive — which can be a strong indicator of an employment relationship under the French “subordination” test.

*Recommendations to Keep the Lottery Legally Compliant*

I’M not suggesting the campaign be scrapped — but I recommend adjusting the structure to clearly separate advertising participation from ride activity, while still meeting your promotional goals.

# *Remove performance criteria (rides and app hours) as eligibility conditions*

These criteria link the prize to ride-hailing activity, making the reward appear like compensation for services.

*Instead*=> Make eligibility conditional only on active participation in the branded advertising program, i.e. having the Bolt stickers on the car and submitting the monthly sticker photo.

 *Example*:

{quote}“All drivers who are part of the Branded Cars program and have submitted their November and December sticker verification photos are automatically entered into the prize draw.”{quote}

This keeps the reward clearly tied to the ad service, not driving volume, and is aligned with the current advertising contract structure (given that in fact, you expect 75% of drivers meeting this threshold).

# *Frame the lottery as a promotional campaign, not a reward for work*

Distinguish the lottery from a “bonus” and present it as a holiday promotional game for brand ambassadors.

Position the draw as a randomised giveaway for eligible participants, without implying performance or sales targets.

*Example*:

{quote}“As part of our festive campaign, we’re celebrating our most visible drivers with a holiday draw. Every eligible Branded Car is entered automatically – it’s our way of saying thank you for your help in promoting the Bolt brand!”{quote}

This aligns with how promotional giveaways are run by brands and avoids employment-like reward structures.

# *Include the legally required disclaimer visibly in all campaign materials*

*Example*:
On any digital banners, flyers, or in-app popups for the lottery:

{quote}“Cette campagne est destinée aux conducteurs participants à la publicité sur véhicule : Publicité pour la centrale de réservation Bolt.”{quote}

I asked where we are going to communicate, to understand the public exposure of the lotttery.

Hi, [~accountid:5c010fa68ce9b546efc49454] it's been a while - sorry! The application of the article 28 of Act on ABW is quite complex. I don’t know the reason of adding this article to CS file. I understand that the CS file is general and applies to all the Bolt verticals. 

After my analysis of this article I recommend *keeping this article 28 in the file as a potential legal basis for ABW inspection and request because this article is relevant for other verticals where Bolt is operating as an intermediary (Bolt Food, Bolt Rides).* 

The article 28 refers not only to the telecommunication services but also to electronic services providers. The last one might be understood very broadly under another Polish Act (ustawa o świadczeniu usług drogą elektroniczną). One of the exemplar electronic services is *API provision* (application programming interface). 

For the full context: This is relevant for Bolt Food Partners who want to integrate their system with ours. Then, we conclude the separate API agreement allowing Partners to integrate their own software t_o accept orders that the users have submitted via the Bolt Food platform and warehouse management system as well as product information management system in order to ensure the provision of accurate information to the clients on the Bolt Food platform_  (more about API see the confluence and contract templates [here|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/LEG/pages/2577203498/Delivery+Terms+Conditions]).

The article 24 of the ABW Act is more general and, in my opinion, needs to be specified by other provisions like art. 28. For Bolt Rentals the Article 28 should *not* apply as in this case Bolt is not providing electronic services (only rental). 

I know that the feedback was submitted to ABW any way. But tbh, I don’t see a specific legal basis for ABW to request the information about Bolt Rentals provisions. It should have been specified by other relevant legal grounds (article 24 is not sufficient in my opinion and art. 28 doesn’t apply to Rentals). 

Hope it’s clear and helpful for you.

Best,

Jola

If a user does not enable two-factor authentication (‘2FA’) in the Bolt App nor updates their phone number in the Bolt App after changing it, and their old phone number is later reassigned by the mobile provider to a new customer, that new customer may inadvertently gain access to the existing Bolt account linked to it. h3. *Driver Communication Draft – CPH Waiting Zones Update*

We need to communicate the upcoming updates to the *in-app* and *TMS waiting zones* clearly and effectively to all drivers. The goal is to ensure understanding of the changes, encourage compliance, and reduce ongoing issues around Copenhagen Airport (CPH).

----

h4. *1. Purpose of the Communication*

* Explain that the changes are being introduced to *reduce congestion* and improve compliance around CPH.
* Emphasize that these updates are based on *direct feedback from CPH, TMS, and local stakeholders* such as Cirkel K.
* Remind drivers that responsible parking and waiting behavior is critical to maintaining a *positive reputation and continued access* to airport areas.

----

h4. *2. Key Changes to Waiting Zones*

*In-App Waiting Zone*

* *Removed:* Havnehytten and the adjacent parking area (identified as a critical hotspot).
* *Expanded:* Further along *Amager Strandvej* and to include a *large parking area near Amagerstrand*.

*TMS Waiting Zone*

* *Expanded:* To provide more space for drivers to wait safely and legally.
* *Removed:* Parking spaces next to *Cirkel K on Amager Landevej*, as these areas have been repeatedly highlighted by CPH and Cirkel K as problematic.

----

h4. *3. Cirkel K on Amager Landevej*

* Cirkel K continues to experience *significant challenges with taxis blocking access to their station*.
* The issue has resulted in *multiple customer complaints* sent to their headquarters.
* Drivers should be reminded that *waiting or parking on Cirkel K property is strictly prohibited*, and violations may lead to formal action or sanctions.
* This must be *clearly emphasized* in the driver announcement 

----

h4. *4. Expected Driver Actions*

* Only wait within the designated areas shown in the updated zones (to be shared in the app and via visuals).
* Do *not* wait or park at *Havnehytten*, *Cirkel K*, or *any private or commercial property* around the airport.
* Follow all signage, avoid blocking entryways, and cooperate with enforcement from CPH or Bolt’s compliance checks.

----

h4. *5. Communication Format*

* Tone: Informative, cooperative, and firm — focus on collaboration and shared responsibility.
* Format:
** Short introduction (why the update matters).
** Bullet points or visuals showing zone changes.
** A “Do’s and Don’ts” section for quick reference.
** Mention of possible consequences for repeated violations.
* Visuals: Include updated maps of both zones with clearly marked restricted areas.

----

*Rejecting this ticket for the following reasons:*

Since this can’t be managed by individual teams, we can’t simply add a GitHub Copilot review by default for everyone.

We have explored two possible approaches, which can provide teams with an opt-in option:
	1.	*YAML configuration file:*
Teams can add themselves to a YAML config file along with their preferred AI reviewer.
A workflow would then use this file to automatically request reviews based on the configuration.
However, currently it’s not possible to request a review from Copilot via the API, only through the UI.
	2.	*GitHub ruleset:*
A ruleset can be created to automatically add Copilot as a reviewer, with exceptions defined as needed.
However, the bypass option was not considered during our tests, which limits this approach.  Additionally, this setup doesn’t support opt-out from the start; teams would need to request exclusion individually after implementation.

*Additional consideration:*
Some team members may prefer not to enable this, as having Copilot as a reviewer could clutter the pull request and make the review process noisier.

* *Benefit for Bolt:* Bolt retains its favorable PSP rates, potentially reducing overall transaction costs.
* *Faster time to market:* Virtua handles all technical implementation and leverages Bolt’s legal presence in each local market to increase time to market.



*Option 2: Virtua Mobility as MOR, Handling All Payment Collection*

In this model, Virtua Mobility assumes full responsibility for all aspects of payment collection. In locations where Virtua has no presence - they would need to register a local entity eg South Africa and Thailand.

* *Payment Processing:* Virtua Mobility manages the entire payment collection process through our integrated PSPs.
* *Virtua Mobility's Role:* We are the sole point of contact for payment processing, handling all merchant accounts, settlement, and reconciliation.
* *Fees:* Virtua Mobility charges a platform technology fee (to be discussed) and passes on all payment processing fees and costs incurred from the PSPs directly to Bolt.
* *Benefit for Bolt:* Simplifies payment operations significantly, as Bolt doesn't need to manage separate PSP relationships. Virtua Mobility handles all the complexities of payment collection.
* *Longer implementation timelines:* Acquiring the rights to operate a physical payment terminal without a legal entity will take longer.

Hey Thiago,
Here is what I found via AI tool research. Do you think any of this has traction to legally challenge the reaction test law in Latvia before every ride? I’ve also added the industry’s position that we discussed with the commission prior to the approval of this legislation.

Here’s a *concise EU-law summary with references* against imposing reaction tests *only* on platform-based shared mobility (but not on car rental/other rental channels):

# *GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679)*
#* *Data minimisation & necessity (Art. 5(1)(c))* — a blanket “test before every ride” on platforms alone is likely disproportionate versus targeted, risk-based controls. ([EUR-Lex|https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/2016-05-04/eng?utm_source=chatgpt.com])
#* *Special-category/health inferences (Art. 9)* — reaction tests can reveal impairment; without a clear legal basis with safeguards, processing may be unlawful. ([EUR-Lex|https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj/eng?utm_source=chatgpt.com])
#* *Automated decisions (Art. 22)* — auto-blocking access based on a test triggers Art. 22 rights (human review, ability to contest, meaningful information); CJEU has underscored the scope of Art. 22 in scoring/automated assessments. ([EUR-Lex|https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX%3A62021CJ0634_RES&utm_source=chatgpt.com])

# *European Accessibility Act (Directive (EU) 2019/882)*

If the test becomes a *gate to the service*, it must be *accessible* (with equivalent alternatives). A selective obligation on platforms risks excluding users with disabilities and breaching accessibility requirements for digital services. ([EUR-Lex|https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/882/oj/eng?utm_source=chatgpt.com])

# *EU Charter of Fundamental Rights — Article 21 (Non-discrimination)*

Treating *comparable services differently* (platform sharing vs. other rental channels) *without objective justification* can amount to indirect discrimination, especially where the test disproportionately affects certain user groups (e.g., disability, older devices). ([EUR-Lex|https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A12012P021&utm_source=chatgpt.com])

# *AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)* _(if any AI is used in the test)_

Not per se banned, but you must *avoid prohibited AI practices* and check whether your system falls under *high-risk* obligations (documentation, human oversight, etc.). A platform-only mandate could impose an uneven regulatory burden absent justification. ([EUR-Lex|https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng?utm_source=chatgpt.com])

# *Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (2005/29/EC)*

If a universal test *adds undue friction* without clear, evidenced safety benefits—and is *selectively* imposed only on platforms—it may be challenged as an *unfair practice* or unjustified obstacle in the consumer journey, per the Directive and Commission guidance. ([EUR-Lex|https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2005/29/oj/eng?utm_source=chatgpt.com])


*Bottom line:* A platform-only reaction-test mandate raises *proportionality (GDPR)*, *accessibility (EAA)*, *non-discrimination (Charter)*, *AI-governance (AI Act)* and *consumer-protection (UCPD)* concerns. Safety goals should be pursued via *targeted, accessible, evidence-based measures applied consistently across comparable services*, not by singling out platform sharing. ([EUR-Lex|https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/2016-05-04/eng?utm_source=chatgpt.com])

[^LMA's position on the draft law proposed by the MoT on reaction tests.pdf]

{quote}We built a Terraform Landing Zone vending machine in house and orchestrate with Jenkins. Been running it this way for maybe 7 years now and we’re currently sitting around 520 accounts.

Separate state files per account.

Each account has a tfvars, there’s another for each business unit, each company, and one globally (along with associated terraform config) so we can ensure changes are applied across multiple segments of the business as required.

Our vpc builder uses ipam and we have three “tshirt sizes” so we don’t have to think about cidrs and subnet configs. It supports TGW so connectivity is there from the start.

It also creates the Okta groups for our standard IAM roles and configures the relevant Okta app.

It also deploys some Cloudformation stacks and triggers the deployment of some of our governance tooling into the account

Someone requests an account, provides some variable values and the size of their vpc if they want one.

Couple of approval steps (line manager and someone from engineering) then Jenkins packages everything up and runs the terraform commands.

About 15-20 minutes later they can login to the IAM role via Okta and start building.{quote}

From the Lithuanian law perspective, the NDA would need to be signed by both parties – the parent or legal guardian on behalf of the minor, and Bolt.

Please note, however, that the enforceability of NDAs signed by minors (through parents) is weak in practice and could be seen as legally uncertain or reputationally unattractive.

As this appears to be a low-risk case, we should prioritise operational safeguards over a formal NDA.

A few simple measures can provide stronger and cleaner protection:

* Allow minors access only to non-sensitive areas.
* Require employees to lock screens, close dashboards, and avoid displaying internal metrics during the visit.
* Keep financial and HR data inaccessible.
* Give visitors a short verbal reminder: “You may see or hear business information; please keep it private.”
* Inform office employees in advance about the shadowing day so they can plan their work accordingly.
* etc.

Hi Alexandra. Thanks for the call and appreciate taking the time. HERE is the PDF I showed you. See summary points below. 

----

*General feedback to consider moving forward*

When there are so many factors to take into account (doors, two boxes, and design continuity across two connected walls), it would’ve been super helpful to receive the designs:

* With the *template still visible as an overlay* (for example, to confirm that the TV is indeed centered in the first section).
* In a *combined view*, showing both designs together to give a full visual impression and make it easier for the client (us) to understand that the two images are actually connected. None of us realized this until today, when we placed the two designs side by side in Keynote.

----

*Feedback on the designs*

* *Wall 1:* As we don’t have any design with the template still kept; can we please confirm that this right-hand section has been trimmed to the exact width so it’s +100% centered around the TV?+
* *Wall 1:* This wall will have a very low attention span and will mainly be seen from a distance (around 10–20 meters away — never closer than 10 with a good angle to read). Travelers will be walking by quickly on their way to baggage claim, and the view will also be partially blocked by pillars and seen from an angle. In its current form, the text is unlikely to be read by many — with pillars in the way and people viewing it from far away and at an angle, visibility will be quite limited. +If possible and design toolkit allows, please make the font bigger.+
* *Wall 1:* The primary area of our entire placement is where the TV is located. Ideally, this is also where we should use our recognizable Bolt Green to create a quick association with the brand. Can we please change this area to Bolt’s standard green? This would, in turn, require reversing the colors in the TV motion graphics. If that makes things too complicated, feel free to keep the dark green as it is — not ideal, but it still works.
* *Wall 2:* All travelers are coming from the right, walking quickly past and alongside this wall. Very few — if any — will look at it straight on. This means that any content placed too close to the left-hand side of the box won’t be fully visible, as it will fall outside the field of view for most travelers passing by. Therefore, I suggest +extending the dark green area and moving the copy slightly to the left+ to create more margin and prevent the “Made in Europe” text from being hidden behind the box
* *Wall 2:* Please change the “Download the Bolt app” to “Made in Europe”. If internal pushback, please move ahead with “Download the Bolt app” as intended. 
* *Wall 2:* When placing the two wall designs next to each other, there appears to be a slight glitch between the images — likely due to bleed margins. Please confirm that this has been accounted for and that the images will align perfectly once installed.
* *TV Motion Graphic:* Please slow it down. Everything moves really quickly (10 sec). The entire loop can easily be twice as long.
* *TV Motion Graphic:* If we are able to change the wall background color to BOlt main green instead of dark green, then please revert the motion graphic so, rather than green background and white text, we go with white background and green text. Again, if this complicates things with your toolkit, feel free to ignore. 
* *TV Motion Graphic:* On the second frame, it should ideally be enough to just show the offer. There’s no need to repeat “All Electric, All Copenhagen,” as it’s already communicated in the first frame and now only takes up unnecessary space and dilutes the message. People will see this screen for a maximum of three seconds — there’s simply too much to take in as it’s currently designed. Please note, this isn’t a comment on the actual design itself — just a heads-up that no one will be able to properly read or absorb the content in its current form because (1) the TV is fairly small and viewed from a distance at a narrow angle, and (2) the second frame is too busy. I hope we can find a way to solve it — and of course, you decide how the design should account for this context.

----

*Final notes*

* Please take this feedback into account as far as possible and within what your toolkit allows. Hopefully, the provided context helps enable a few adjustments — even if slightly outside the technical limits of the design toolkit, which is meant to support, not restrict, design optimization. If you get internal pushback, make a call yourself and we’ll move forward with it.
* Also, acknowledging that local teams could’ve done a better job filtering feedback from Local Ops. Going forward, we’ll be stricter gatekeepers so you can work with more confidence and fewer people involved (Robin will be the main POC).
* Lastly, while this placement is tricky, local teams should’ve done a better job explaining how travelers actually sees and consumes it — from what angle, distance, and how quickly attention fades. That context should ideally inform the design (font size, copy amount, etc.). We’ll take that as a learning for next time.

----

+*UPDATE (13.11)*+

* We have now been asked to provide comments on the SLA with Virtua ([+LINK+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1O7UQJzQAACEujR3XSiGaAr8_vPxC3pGZDh06UhCcmX4/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.cy383587blpe]).
** NB. This no longer appears to be just a ‘Heads of Terms’. Instead, it now appears to be a draft of the full Integration Agreement.
** Virtua is a software and hardware provider. Virtua will also be responsible for collecting payments from riders.
** InfoSec is currently reviewing Virtua on a separate ticket.
** Virtua gateway is available in Australia, Austria, Belgium, Canada, Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, Malaysia, Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Portugal, Singapore, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, United Kingdom, United States, Japan (beta), and Poland. Also in Ukraine, Malta, Thailand and South Africa.
** Preferred model to adopt is where Virtua is the Merchant of Record, handling all payment collection.
*** “_In this model, Virtua Mobility assumes full responsibility for all aspects of payment collection_” - Virtua manages the entire payment collection process through our integrated PSPs.
* I had a call with Ankita to discuss (i) adoption of the API model; and (ii) differences from Tapbox setup.
** In short - she does not know. 
*** Legal has previously explained to the business that the API model does not quite work - Even though the kiosk provider has access to the API, they are not providing the details of a fixed number of people; instead, use of Bolt’s services will be open to the public at large. 
*** However, business are still keen to push ahead. Current draft is likely to change, but it is what we have for now.
** I agreed with Ankita that I would include some provisional data sharing protections in the agreement - as having something is better than nothing - with the caveat that I still need my Qs confirmed before I can finalise my input.

+*THOUGHTS*+

* Agreement ([LINK|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1O7UQJzQAACEujR3XSiGaAr8_vPxC3pGZDh06UhCcmX4/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.6zeyohruldjb]):
** Agreement is between Bolt Ops OU and a UAE Kiosk Provider (Virtua).
** Agreement sets a global framework under which Virtua leases kiosks to Bolt, and Bolt provides access to the Rider Booker API.
*** Virtua will provide Bolt-branded software designed to operate exclusively within Bolt’s ecosystem. Virtua will also provide 24/7 software support for incidents and patches. Virtua will also collect payments in its own name and remit the collected amounts to Bolt on a monthly basis.
** Clause 11.2 currently contains a mutual indemnity and refers to a DSA at Schedule 2 (which does not exist).
*** Clause 12.2 also contains a liability cap pf 2x fees ⚠️ 
** Ride Booker API Schedule contains a DSA Annex.
*** Parties are ICs in relation to driver and passenger data. Does not mention any payment information ⚠️ 
*** If A28 agreement is needed, the parties will enter one.
*** Immediate notification of PDBs. However, no mention of DSRRs, audit rights, or reg inquiry assistance ⚠️ 
*** Mentions international transfers / SCCs, but could go into more detail with Annexes ⚠️ 
** +*Conclusion*+: 
*** Given that this is not quite the usual API setup (and so we need proper protections), but also that we need something practical that will fit this halfway house, IMO the best approach would be to include out full suite of usual data sharing provisions (rather than the more limited API DSA). 
*** This will at least give us a strong _starting basis_. We can adapt it as needed going forward.
* Controller vs processor debate:
** In the context of payment collection, I think ultimately Virtua is more likely to be a controller here, particularly as it is the merchant of record.
*** Virtua collects payments in its own name before relaying them to Bolt on a monthly basis: “_Virtua acts on its own behalf (it is not a payment institution or payment agent of Bolt)_”.
** With regards to the remaining elements of user data processing, there are arguments for both controller and processor:
*** C: Per Clause 3.2(b), Virtua has a limited privacy notice ([here|https://www.virtuamobility.com/privacy-policy]), but it is minimal and seems to apply more to Bolt representatives. Virtua has access to the ridebooker API to ‘enable’ ride requests (hence the ridebooker API Addendum).
*** P: According to Clause 3.3, Virtua “_provides a technology interface only. It does not act as agent, broker, dispatcher or representative of Bolt, any Passenger, or any Provider; has no authority to bind any of them; does not control Provider selection, pricing or performance_”.
*** +*Conclusion*+: Ultimately, the latter point will depend on (a) whether Virtua uses the data for its own purposes / storage at all (including whether Virtua relies on its own PN); and (b) to what extent we want to rely on the API integration model. 
*** To keep things moving (and given the current use of API structures), IMO we should proceed with pro-Bolt independent controller provisions (with some minor tweaks to resemble the key points of the API DSA), as this is the least messy approach. We can then adapt this as needed when more info comes in ✅ 
*** For good measure, I have also included a term in the main agreement stating that if required, we will enter a separate DPA.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Questions:
** Do we know if Virtua is using the data for its own purposes at all? Not just with payments, but more generally? Does Virtua store driver and passenger data on its own systems, and does it have a privacy notice / T&Cs of its own?
* Steps:
** (1) Confirm controller / processor position.
*** POCs to confirm whether Virtua will be using the data for its own purposes / storing data on its own systems / relying on its own privacy notice ([+LSS-58344+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-58344]).
** (2) Tweak DSA / prepare DPA as needed.
*** Main issues with current draft are *mutual / capped indemnity*, incomplete *data processing information*, no *DSRRs/audits/reg inquiries*, and no *international data transfer* Annex. Provided that these are addressed, we can go either way.
