Internal notes for the team:

*Background*: The team is working with a group of researchers to put together a proposal to apply for EU funds. The main research goals are (1) improve road safety for pedestrians, cyclists, and other micro-mobility users and (2) increase use of active and micromobility modes in all ages and socioeconomic groups as a result of higher safety.

At this stage, Bolt will be sharing a concept of what Bolt can provide to a consortium, namely e-scooter camera footage of accidents to analyse accident causation. Bolt does not have computer vision capabilities to analyse footage and classify accidents - this can be covered by AI provider [CIRCE|https://www.fcirce.es/en/strategic-lines/ai-and-digitalization], a member of the research group.

Currently, we have only two cities where we run e-scooter dashcams: Oslo and Washington; legal analysis of local requirements and recommendations can be found [here|https://taxify.atlassian.net/issues?jql=textfields%20~%20%22dashboard%20cameras%2A%22&selectedIssue=PRIV-247]. 

*Issues:*

# *Use of dashcam footage for research and improvement purposes*

We only mention in the Privacy Notices that we use dashcam footage for safety and security purpose ('_To enable and provide safety features_'). We should update the Privacy Notices to include the use of dashcam footage for research and improvement of the Bolt services ('_To perform research, testing, and analytics to better understand and improve our business and the Bolt services_'). New purpose closely relates to the original purpose - we should be able to rely on the legitimate interest (LIA to be drafted).

# *Retention requirements*

Issue: While there is no specific requirement related to the retention of dashcam footage under current US federal or DC law, Norwegian authorities advise companies to retain video recording for 7 days or retain video recordings for the duration of ongoing investigations or claims, up to 30 days. 

Solution: Extend current retention periods beyond 30 days for scientific and research purposes provided that full anonymisation is applied + Privacy Notice disclosures. 

# *Sharing footage with third parties*

Issue: May require consent or legal obligation as a valid legal basis. Solution: anonymisation - blur identifiable individuals and license plates, limit the length of the footage to the relevant accident. Transparency via Privacy Notice. 

# *Use of AI provider*

_AI governance_. We need to go through vendor onboarding and preferably review technical docs re their computer vision model.

_Privacy and Data Protection_. Contract should cover: audit rights, liability in the event of a gross error, privacy clauses (DPA), guarantee that the AI provider will not reuse our data inappropriately, and security obligations. 

# *Privacy assessments and AI assessment*

PPRA, LIA, DPIA + AI assessment?

*Advise to the team:* 

* Data sharing is feasible provided that relevant user disclosures, data anonymisation  and contractual safeguards with AI provider are put in place.
* Privacy assessments can run in parallel. AI provider should agree to help us with the relevant DPIA and AI assessments.

h3. What *Workona* (and similar tools like *Toby*) do

Both are browser-based workspace managers built primarily as Chrome extensions.

*Core functionality:*

* Let users organize and save browser tabs into “workspaces” or “projects.”
* Sync those workspaces to the cloud so you can reopen all your tabs later or across devices.
* Offer search, sharing, and sometimes collaboration features (e.g., share a workspace with a team).
* Integrate with Google Drive, Slack, Notion, etc.

h3. 🔍 How they technically work

* The Chrome extension requests broad permissions such as:
** _“Read your browsing history”_
** _Access to cookies and session storage_
* These permissions allow the extension to detect:
** Open tabs
** Save tab’s URLs
** Titles, and 
** Metadata like favicons, timestamps, and (depending on the site) workspace tags.
* That data is sent to Workona’s or Toby’s cloud backend, usually hosted on AWS or Firebase, for synchronization.

h3. ⚠️ Privacy & security risks

h4. 1. :green_circle: *Data exposure of internal or confidential URLs*

If a user saves tabs pointing to internal systems (e.g., Bolt’s Confluence, Jira, internal dashboards, prototypes, or even draft product specs), those URLs are synced to the vendor’s servers.

* Even without page content, *URLs can show sensitive info*, project names, identifiers, query parameters, customer IDs, etc.
* The vendor  becomes a processor - [DPA |https://workona.com/compliance/dpa/]needs to be signed

h4. 2. :green_circle: *Vendor compliance posture*

* No EU data residency 
* Retention or deletion after the account is deleted

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Hey [~accountid:712020:8fd75aa8-dcfb-42ad-93ab-53900ee4c301] I can see that the Legal Representative asserted new court judgments to support their claim. I’ve done a quick ChatGPT research. They seem to match the current situation. Both cases involved damage to motor vehicle caused by a rented e-scooter. 



*Landgericht Hamburg – 16 August 2022, case no. 4 C 18/22*

* The court held that the owner of the car may have a right to _information_ from the scooter-rental operator for the identity of the last user (renter) of the e-scooter to start a claim for damages.
* The judgment (or at least the commentary about it) supports that under certain conditions the user/renter of a scooter can be required to be identified by the operator/owner for the purposes of pursuing a damage claim.

*Landgericht Berlin II, 22 October 2024 – case no. 22 S 6/23 (2)*

* The user of the e-scooter (and/or the provider) owes the injured party a direct claim under insurance law (specifically § 115 VVG – direct claim against the liability insurer of the vehicle).



To me, this looks like a valid legal basis, however, I’m not sure of the legal status of court judgments in Germany. I.e. without a provision in law, can we rely on court judgment?

Hi team, 

The user is reporting a double-charge because of incremental authorization.
Incremental authorization in card payments refers to the process of requesting an additional authorization on a customer’s card when the original authorized amount is insufficient to cover the final transaction cost. Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Hi [~accountid:712020:bc7bca9c-4d13-42b6-9684-04014a47f7aa] Yes, exactly - that’s the kind of thing meant here. Bolt should take whatever reasonable steps it considers necessary to verify that the alleged “bad actor” is actually at fault. There’s no one-size-fits-all approach, it depends on the circumstances.

For instance, we might ask the one complaining for evidence (like screenshots of messages, ensuring no personal information is included), request information from the accused party, or review relevant data such as driver ratings or trip history.

That said, we don’t *_have_* to take any particular action unless we’re obliged to for transport-related or (in our opinion) safety reasons. The key point is simply that, if we do act, we should have some independent basis for our decision rather than relying solely on what someone else reports.

Put another way, if a regulator later asks, “Why did you block this person?” and our only answer is “because someone told us to,” that would not reflect well on us.

Hope this helps!

~ Analysis ~

h3. *1. Introduction*

I am analysing whether Bolt may legally deploy the Driver Queue Optimiser (DQO) feature in the Thai market under current data protection and regulatory laws, with a focus on the Personal Data Protection Act B.E. 2562 (2019) (PDPA).

The DQO algorithm dynamically determines driver-to-rider matching based on factors such as rider wait time, request frequency, driver proximity, and traffic conditions. The system operates without direct human involvement and may indirectly affect driver earnings.

h3. *2. Key Legal Considerations Under Thai Law*

h4. 2.1 No Prohibition on Automated Decision-Making (ADM)

Unlike the EU’s GDPR (Article 22), the Thai PDPA does not include an explicit restriction or prohibition on decisions made solely by automated means.

* There is no statutory requirement for human intervention, explanation, or opt-out mechanisms in the context of ADM.
* The concept of a "significant effect" (e.g., material income loss) triggering additional obligations is not present in Thai law.

h4. 2.2 General Principles Still Apply

While ADM is not directly regulated, general PDPA principles must still be respected.

h4. 2.3 Regulatory Guidance

To date, the Thai Personal Data Protection Committee (PDPC) has not issued specific guidance, enforcement decisions, or public commentary on ADM or algorithmic fairness.

I have reviewed the guidance specific to ride-hailing services, and I have not found any provision that would be a blocker to this initiative. 

h3. *3. Conclusion and Recommendation*

Thailand's legal framework currently permits the deployment of DQO *without regulatory blockers* under the PDPA.

* There is *no ADM-specific prohibition*, threshold, or consent requirement.

h3. *4. Conclusion and Recommendation*

*Recommendation:* Proceed with the DQO deployment in Thailand. Internal testing (e.g., with Josef Kurchishvili’s team) should still be conducted to avoid any mistakes on our side.

Following your recent questions, I’ve conducted further research into the relevant legal framework, TfL's operator/driver handbooks and public guidance, as well as the limited available case law in this area. I've set out below a clear explanation of why Bolt is potentially exposed under the Equality Act 2010 in this specific scenario, along with an assessment of our legal risk, options for defence, and a recommended path forward.

----

h3. Why Bolt May Be Liable under the Equality Act 2010

# *Statutory Framework – Section 29 of the Equality Act 2010*
Under Section 29(1) and (2), service providers (including PHV operators) must not discriminate against the public in the provision of services. This includes direct discrimination (s.13), failure to make reasonable adjustments (s.20), and harassment or victimisation.
# *Bolt as a PHV Operator*
Bolt holds a PHV Operator Licence from TfL and accepts bookings directly from passengers. As such, we are considered a *service provider* under the Equality Act and may be held responsible for discriminatory conduct arising during service delivery.
# *Section 164A – Duty on All PHV Drivers*
This provision applies to *all* PHV drivers (not just those with WAVs). It requires:
#* The carriage of disabled passengers and their wheelchairs (where reasonably possible),
#* Reasonable mobility assistance,
#* No additional charge for doing so.
This duty applies unless the driver holds a *medical exemption under s.166* — which is *not the case here*.
# *Section 165 – Additional Duties for WAV Drivers Only*
This section imposes a duty to carry passengers *while seated in their wheelchair*, secure the wheelchair, and provide additional assistance.
It applies *only to designated WAV drivers*, which this driver is not.

----

h3. 🔎 Application to This Case

* The driver had *no s.166 exemption* so the s.164A duty applies.
* The recorded cancellation reason was explicitly discriminatory: “passengers with wheelchairs”.
* The driver did *not engage or offer assistance*, but cancelled immediately.
* The journey was accepted and matched via Bolt’s platform, meaning the act of discrimination occurred *in the context of a service Bolt agreed to provide*.

On that basis, Bolt is *potentially liable under s.29* for failing to ensure the rider was not subjected to discrimination in accessing a booked service.

----

h3. 🧭 Legal Exposure and Risk

*Key Risk Factors:*

* Explicit discriminatory cancellation reason.
* No legal basis for the refusal (no exemption).
* No effort to engage or assist the passenger (a key requirement under s.164A).
* Platform design (i.e. lack of WAV category or disclosures regarding limitations, yet allows bookings by wheelchair users) arguably fails to adequately accommodate wheelchair users.

*Legal Risk:*

* The facts support a strong claim of *direct discrimination* and *failure to make reasonable adjustments*.
* *High regulatory scrutiny*: TfL has been informed.
* The £12,100 claim is *credible* – it's within the *upper range of Vento Band 1* (injury to feelings for first-time incidents with aggravating factors).

----

h3. 🛡 Defence Options

While we can raise mitigating points (e.g. unsuitable vehicle, no prior complaints, rider got a second vehicle soon after, swift driver suspension), the defence remains *weak*.

Further, we would likely need to *instruct external counsel* to handle this matter due to the Equality Act implications and the public sensitivity. Realistically, *legal costs could £5,000-£10,000 (even pre-litigation)*, without a guaranteed outcome. That money could instead fund a pragmatic settlement.

----

h3. 📌 Recommendation

# *Offer a without prejudice settlement* in the range of *£1,500–£2,000*, acknowledging the rider's distress without admitting liability. That said, *the final settlement figure is up to you and the business* — we could try a lower initial offer if you think appropriate. I'm happy to discuss your thoughts on this.
# *Review our accessibility features* on the platform:
#* Consider implementing a dedicated *WAV category*. (I’ve checked – *Uber offers this*.)
#* At minimum, ensure *clearer disclosures* around vehicle suitability for non-folding wheelchairs.

Hi [~accountid:712020:910c9a84-3532-4a39-97d2-4aee154ce8df], thank you!

You’re right that the applicable model isn’t determined by where a driver lives or is licensed, but by where each trip commences — i.e. the pick-up point.

*In London, only the Principal Model applies*. Since you have confirmed the pick-up address was in London, we can safely assume it is the principal model that applies here (as will always be the case for London only).

Outside London, in cities where *Flex (Agency Model)* has been launched, both models are available. Drivers in those locations can choose which product to operate under in-app — either *Standard (Principal)* or *Flex (Agency)* — and may therefore move between the two models depending on the ride type selected and where the trip starts.

In short, what matters is *how and where the ride is ordered*, not where the driver is based, and the same driver can operate under different models if they drive in multiple cities. London is the exception and we can always assume it will be principal model if the pick-up location is London.

I hope that makes sense! 🙂

The reason I suggested running this past Safety (Sarra / Central Ops) is because of potential safety-related implications rather than privacy ones.

In this case, the driver only completed two trips that day. Even if we broaden the timeframe (e.g. 11:00-19:00), the driver will inevitably send us recordings covering both trips. Since he knows one of them involved a complaint, he will easily deduce which passenger filed it. This effectively undermines any privacy mitigation and could create a safety risk for the rider, as it may expose their identity in the driver’s eyes. In addition to that, we’d be receiving redundant data (i.e. recording of two trips instead of one).

That’s why I’d like Safety to confirm whether sharing the trip-level timeframe, even in a broader window, is acceptable from their side, or whether we should maintain the usual approach of not disclosing trip identifiers in such cases.

Hope that’s clear but let me know in case you have any questions.

Hello,

The customer used an APM (Alternative Payment Method) to place the order and this type of payment methods does not have a preauthorisation option that is later reversed. They only support a direct charge on the card. So if the user makes an order but then cancels it, in this case we refund their money unlike preauthorisation where we just release the reserved amount. 
So in this case, the user placed an order and we charged them higher, but at the end of the ride, the order price decreased or the order is cancelled, so automatically we refunded them the difference. But later on from your end (CS) you initiated a full refund, which was applied to the first higher order amount. And this is what creates the debt as the balance thinks that we have returned the full amount to the user, meaning whatever the user previously paid was all returned to them. But since a service was provided to the user for the order or cancellation fee, it is still trying to charge the user for the extra refunded amount. That is where the debt comes from.

The Payments engineering team is aware of the issue and is exploring ways to help fix this.
In the meantime, could you complete a refund to the user’s balance on a different order to compensate for the debt in their account?

Analysis:

h3. *1. Introduction*

I am analysing whether Bolt may legally deploy the Driver Queue Optimiser (DQO) feature in the Thai market under current data protection and regulatory laws, with a focus on the Personal Data Protection Act B.E. 2562 (2019) (PDPA).

The DQO algorithm dynamically determines driver-to-rider matching based on factors such as rider wait time, request frequency, driver proximity, and traffic conditions. The system operates without direct human involvement and may indirectly affect driver earnings.

h3. *2. Key Legal Considerations Under Thai Law*

h4. 2.1 No Prohibition on Automated Decision-Making (ADM)

Unlike the EU’s GDPR (Article 22), the Thai PDPA does not include an explicit restriction or prohibition on decisions made solely by automated means.

* There is no statutory requirement for human intervention, explanation, or opt-out mechanisms in the context of ADM.
* The concept of a "significant effect" (e.g., material income loss) triggering additional obligations is not present in Thai law.

h4. 2.2 General Principles Still Apply

While ADM is not directly regulated, general PDPA principles must still be respected.

h4. 2.3 Regulatory Guidance

To date, the Thai Personal Data Protection Committee (PDPC) has not issued specific guidance, enforcement decisions, or public commentary on ADM or algorithmic fairness.

I have reviewed the guidance specific to ride-hailing services, and I have not found any provision that would be a blocker to this initiative.

h3. *3. Conclusion and Recommendation*

Thailand's legal framework currently permits the deployment of DQO *without regulatory blockers* under the PDPA.

* There is *no ADM-specific prohibition*, threshold, or consent requirement.

h3. *4. Conclusion and Recommendation*

*Recommendation:* Proceed with the DQO deployment in Thailand. Internal testing (e.g., with Josef Kurchishvili’s team) should still be conducted to avoid any mistakes on our side.

+*UPDATE (14.11)*+

* I have found a Slack channel ([here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C0460RJ5QEP/p1761751268308059]) discussing the launch of WfW in Germany. Ernesto is on the channel (and so it seems he is already aware) but no-one from the Privacy Team is.
* Based on a quick skim of the channel:
** We are partnering with a Berlin fleet to launch WfW in Germany. For the pilot phase, it will be a new scheduled rides category ('G-Cars for Women').
** In Germany, driver licences and ID cards do not have gender listed on them. However, there is a gender field on passports.
*** In July, discussions were had ([link|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C0460RJ5QEP/p1753190288693159]) regarding introducing an additional layer of verification for riders - asking them to upload a copy of their passports. However, it was pointed out that not all riders will be carrying a passport. As such, it appears that scope was expanded to IDs as well (even though these do not have a gender field), although +*_this is not clear_*+. It was either that or not verify at all (i.e., IDs would primarily be a deterrent). Discussion then turned ([here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C0460RJ5QEP/p1761751268308059]) to other means of checking gender, given that people are generally reluctant to share such sensitive documents. Ultimately, it sounds like we may be going with passports.
** Dawit was looped into this in July, and according to Ops “_no concerns were expressed… In the launch confluence, there is not mention of a privacy team, thus this was not done yet_”.
*** Apparently this was not addressed with Legal via an SD ticket. It was addressed in meetings and via the above Slack channel.
** Dovile has expressed a willingness to give us time for review, which is good: “_if we need to push the pilot because of the need to check these things, I'll be happy to do so. We have been working on this internally for a while and my main priority is to do this in the best possible and compliant manner_”.
* Preliminary Thoughts:
** See previous high-level analysis. Generally ok to launch from a privacy POV, even though the feature itself is problematic.
** Main issue here is the *collection of passport*, which appears to be happening on the rider side. As such, this is the main issue to consider.
*** Re local laws on processing ID docs - There are some specific laws on copying ID docs (e.g., [ID Law|https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/englisch_pauswg/englisch_pauswg.html#p0185]). Generally, it seems advisable to rely on user *consent* to do this (this should be fine, given that we would probably delete it upon receipt of a deletion request anyway), and not pass copies on to any third parties. Since consent can be withdrawn, it is advisable to make a note of the gender as part of manual review (in case deleted), and to honour consent withdrawals (users can then re-upload if needed) ⚠️ 
*** Could be regarded as excessive unless absolutely necessary ⚠️  This will depend on whether other methods are available. We would need to be specific and clear on why we are asking the user for their passport, and what will be done with it. (We cannot practically ask riders to redact / cover up certain info).
*** Retention of copies of ID could also be viewed as unjustified ⚠️ ideal approach would be to extract the gender field and delete the rest. If we keep it, it must be clearly marked as a copy.
*** If we are checking the ID docs automatically, then there is a risk of both ADM and errors/inaccuracy (also if processing biometrics of facial imagery, then A9 risks) ⚠️ 
** There is also the issue of agreements with the fleet, but presumably this will be addressed as part of the wider T&Cs project.
* Next Steps:
** Questions:
*** Are we collecting passport of drivers in addition to riders? If not, what is being decided based on my advice from the current ticket?
** I have asked Dovile to create a ticket for Privacy with all the relevant info. Since we have som wiggle room re timing, I have also asked that she wait for my review ([link|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C0460RJ5QEP/p1763117767012959?thread_ts=1761751268.308059&cid=C0460RJ5QEP]).

Napkin math: 
We do average of 580 refund per h. (scr 1) by AI
Additionally, we receive around 2.7k RED compensation cases per day = 112 per h
BUT. Let’s not forget about *yellow* cases which are escalated anyway and would be refunded in this case.
There are ~2.3K cases of the sort daily = 95 cases per h


Support comp eligibility being down for an hour would result in extra 660 (580 + 0.7 AR * 112) cases being escalated.
With average 2.5€ case cost, we have 1650€ per hour.


Alternatively, we’d have refunded extra 207 cases, not adjusting for fraud possibility 
This would be a cost of 207 * 3.5 = 724€. (minus escalation costs for ~100 cases = 250€) = 470€


So with escalation, in theory *we lose 1200€ more.* Prolly makes sense to add a dynamic config there to control it.

The problem with its report is that the query, which sets up the report, is too massive. It has several common table expressions (CTEs), and they all select 5 years of data. 
There is a filter for the report on declaration date, but that filter is not pushed down to the CTEs. So every time you run this report, it has to process 5 years of data on several tables. And that amount is growing over time. The report will eventually fail either with the configured timeout of 10 minutes or the configured memory limit of 500GB.

Maybe the creators of this underlying view for this report can help you. For example, an easy fix would be to set the hardcoded filter that selects the past 5 years a bit to the future, so it would select only from the past year.

Hello,

The customer used an APM (Alternative Payment Method) to place the order and this type of payment methods does not have a preauthorisation option that is later reversed. They only support a direct charge on the card. So if the user makes an order but then cancels it, in this case we refund their money unlike preauthorisation where we just release the reserved amount. 
So in this case, the user placed an order and we charged them higher, but at the end of the ride, the order price decreased or the order is cancelled, so automatically we refunded them the difference. But later on from your end (CS) you initiated a full refund, which was applied to the first higher order amount. And this is what creates the debt as the balance thinks that we have returned the full amount to the user, meaning whatever the user previously paid was all returned to them. But since a service was provided to the user for the order or cancellation fee, it is still trying to charge the user for the extra refunded amount. That is where the debt comes from.

The Payments engineering team is aware of the issue and is exploring ways to help fix this.
In the meantime, could you complete a refund to the user’s balance on a different order to compensate for the debt in their account?

We had a “workshop” yesterday with [~accountid:622f787a1f014e0069cc0d85] where we created a test account for  EE Bolt Market. Summary of the Safety gate system and initial thoughts:

* Main admin: There can be only one “main” admin. Main admin is the person who can create profiles for each entity/BM store and add users under each entity’s dashboard. Main admin can also assign local admins who can manage the dashboard info about the legal entity, add users under the entity profile, etc. Since [~accountid:622f787a1f014e0069cc0d85] has created back in the day account already for the same system which covers the Safety Gate then she could stay as the main admin. 
** Problem with above solution: Mian account is linked to Kiriska’s personal phone and phone number. If she would leave at some point then main admin’s account should be linked to some other phone & phone number (yes, account is actually linked to specific phone as well). 
It would be ofc possible to create totally new account with some generic email address, phone number etc which belongs to the company and to which relevant teams would have access to. The problem with this:  We have a “company” phone and phone number. Since this is used in all possible public registers, then it is turned off most of the time and in the safe. If we would use the same phone and phone number then we should decide which teams have access to it.

*QUESTION 1*: *should we keep* [~accountid:622f787a1f014e0069cc0d85] *from Legal OPs as the main admin or create main admin profile with generic company credentials?*

* Local admins: For testing purposes I was added as a local admin for EE Bolt Market.  This means that I can add “usual” users for the entity dashboard. Users can see probably cases opened against the entity under which they have been added and probably also submit  reports about unsafe products for this specific entity. 
** We should be able to assign several local admins for local entity. Proposal would be: add as local admins one person from Safety team and one person from product legal team. That way we can make sure that if any safety or legal help is needed for responses, etc relevant teams have full overview and access to the system if e.g. Kirsika should be OOO. 

*QUESTION 2: Do you agree adding one POC from safety team and product legal team under each BM profile as the local admins?*

* Users: As mentioned we can add users under each legal entity. Question - should we add there relevant POC for each local Bolt Market team? Or system should be handled only by safety and legal team? Ideally I would add some POCs from BM teams to increase additional manning work legal/safety might otherwise do to report unsafe products. Ideally Bolt Market teams should submit those reports themselves after consulting with safety team. 
** Why consulting with safety teem is needed? - because on the report form there is a mandatory field of adding a risk assessment. Hey Team,

Mr. Borg’s argument essentially hinges on three points:

# Funds were debited, not just held, before the ride was cancelled — contradicting Bolt’s claim of no charge.
# The app allegedly showed a driver was assigned before failing, suggesting a contract had been formed.
# There are inconsistencies in Bolt’s system data, raising doubt about Bolt’s conclusion that no contract was formed or glitch occurred.

From our end, I believe it is safe to reaffirm the following points:

* Per Bolt’s Passenger T&Cs, a transport contract is only formed upon driver acceptance.
* If no driver accepted, then there was no contract, and no legal obligation to deliver the service.
* Pre-authorisation holds are common industry practice and are not “charges” unless service is provided.
* The refund timing being later than the authorisation is not a sign of a glitch — rather, this reflects the bank's payment processing timelines.

However, these arguments must now be supported with clear evidence.

In my POV, since this topic has MCCAA mediation, and since this trip was actually scheduled in advance and canceled last minute, we should show goodwill to the customer. Maybe a reasonable offer will help resolve the matter quickly. For example, offering €20–€30 voucher or credit as a goodwill token, while making clear it's not an admission of fault.

This is my proposed response:



_Dear Mr. Spiteri,_

_Thank you for your follow-up regarding the consumer complaint submitted by Mr. Michael Borg. We appreciate the opportunity to clarify the situation further and respond to the additional points raised by the consumer._

_Below is our updated response based on a thorough review of our internal system data and payment logs._

# *_Booking and Payment Overview:_* _Mr. Borg scheduled a ride through the Bolt app for the early morning of 12 September 2025. The initial booking was placed through his account, and following its cancellation, additional booking attempts were made via his spouse’s account. We confirm the following:_

* _All attempted ride bookings—whether through Mr. Borg’s or his spouse’s accounts—were subject only to_ *_pre-authorisation holds_*_, not completed charges._
* _Mr. Borg’s payment card is linked to his spouse’s account, and thus the holds appeared on his payment method._
* _Pre-authorisation timestamps:_
** *_04:00:01_* _– €9.80 hold (released_ *_04:00:52_*_)_
** *_04:01:54_* _– €14.00 hold (released_ *_04:03:47_*_)_
** *_04:30:00_* _– €7.60 hold (released_ *_04:34:00_*_)_

_These holds are standard authorisations to confirm payment method validity. The holds were automatically released after each ride request failed due to lack of driver availability. The release of funds may reflect a slight delay depending on the user’s banking provider (in this case, Revolut), but our system confirms that no funds were captured._

# *_No Driver Assignment or Contract Formation:_* _Our system logs confirm that in none of the attempted bookings was a driver assigned or a ride accepted. While the app may briefly indicate that it is locating a driver, no acceptance occurred. As per our Passenger Terms and Conditions:_

* _A ride booking is considered confirmed only upon driver acceptance._
* _Where no driver accepts the request, no transport contract is formed._

_We further confirm that our system experienced_ *_no technical glitch_* _during these transactions. The user interface behaved as expected, returning a "no driver available" status once all nearby drivers declined or ignored the requests._

# *_Clarification Regarding System Consistency:_* _We acknowledge the consumer's concerns around the timing of fund releases and the display of driver search status. We assure you that our technical records align with expected platform functionality, and no inconsistencies or malfunctions were detected._
# *_Customer Experience and Goodwill:_* _While no binding contract was formed and Bolt is not legally liable for consequential expenses, we recognise that Mr. Borg’s experience was frustrating and disruptive. As a gesture of goodwill and without admission of liability, we are prepared to offer a_ *_€25 Bolt app credit_* _to Mr. Borg to acknowledge the inconvenience._

_We hope this clarifies our position and demonstrates our commitment to customer satisfaction and responsible platform conduct. Please let us know if any further details are required._

_With regard to your query below, we understand that the client provides food delivery service mainly in Europe and Africa. The client has obtained trademark registration for Bolt Food in Class 9, 35, 39, and 43 for relevant goods and services. However, there is no trademark registration in China for goods such as insulated bags in Class 21. We understand that the bags would not be actually for sale to the public. The client manufactures bags by using local factories in China and exports them under the mode of OEM.Regarding your questions:1. In order to obtain protection by enforcing the IP rights at the Customs, the right holder should fulfill an independent IPR registration procedure at the GACC (General Administration of Customs of China). We searched the trademark Reg No 53054446 in the system and found the trademark is recorded with an effective period from August 29, 2022 to August 27, 2031 (please see the attached).With the IPR customs registration, there are two methods for the Customs to enforce the IP right. The first one is to detain or take other actions based on the right holder’s application. Once detecting export or import of goods is suspected of infringement, the right holder may report to the Customs, provide relevant guarantees, and request for detention of the goods. As this would require accurate clues and investigation beforehand, it is rare for the right holder to chase and detain the import/export of infringing goods. In practice, it’s more common for the Customs to take Ex Officio action on the infringing goods, which is the second method to enforce the IP right. When the Customs department discovers that imported/exported goods are suspected of infringement upon IP rights in the record, it will notify the right holder of the possible infringement. And the right holder should inform the Customs whether to detain the goods in three working days. If yes, it should also provide relevant guarantees. Hence, we think the risk of detention by the right holder’s report is not high, but there is a chance that the Customs will discover the exportation of Bolt Food bags and inform the right holder.2. We agreed that goods manufactured under the OEM mode do not constitute infringement upon registered trademark in China, because the goods either have a chance to enter the Chinese market and or be available to the Chinese customers. The trademark affixed on the goods is not identified by the public, let alone causing confusion as to the source of the products. This opinion and determination have occurred in precedents of court cases, we believe the court’s opinion in precedents would have a certain effect on the determination in similar cases in the_ [+_future.In_+|http://future.In] _case the goods are detained by the Customs, the client can request to release the goods with a margin and provide evidence proving the goods do not constitute infringement. The evidence could be the OEM manufacture agreement of the bags, trademark registration certificate of Bolt Food in the destination country/territory, and other materials that can prove all of the goods are solely to be exported. For example, the amount of manufactured products indicated in the agreement conforms to the amount of exportation. In practice, if there is solid evidence proving the non-infringement, the Customs will release the goods. In some complex cases, the Customs will tend to deny the infringement and inform the right holder to bring a lawsuit before the Court, and they will take necessary action based on the court’s order. In case the right holder doesn’t file a relevant request with the court within a prescribed period, the Custom will release the goods.3. Unfortunately, the trademark was registered on June 21, 2022, which is not available to a non-use cancellation yet as it’s registered for less than three years. Since the client hasn’t used the trademark in China on relevant goods in Class 21, we’re afraid that the chance of an invalidation request is not high. The applicant is a company called Dongguan Jishan Fruit Distribution Co., Ltd. (东莞市技膳水果配送有限公司) based in Dongguan, Guangdong Province. Did the client have any transaction with this company? Hi Jasmina,

I've reviewed the proposed lottery structure and, from a legal standpoint (particularly under French labour law),I have reclassification concerns due to the way the reward is currently linked to driver performance on the Bolt app.

*Legal Risk in the Current Proposal*

The current setup — requiring 4 rides and 15 hours of weekly app connection to qualify — may appear modest, but it introduces performance-based eligibility criteria for receiving a benefit. This could be interpreted by a court as Bolt:

* *Controlling the driver’s activity (via thresholds and monitoring),*
* *Rewarding use of the Bolt platform rather than participation in a separate advertising service,*
* *And thus, creating an indirect exclusivity or dependency that weakens the independence of the driver.*

When combined with a substantial reward (€9,000), this starts to look more like a structured bonus scheme than a pure advertising incentive — which can be a strong indicator of an employment relationship under the French “subordination” test.

*Recommendations to Keep the Lottery Legally Compliant*

 I recommend adjusting the structure to clearly separate advertising participation from ride activity, while still meeting your promotional goals.

# *Remove performance criteria (rides and app hours) as eligibility conditions*

These criteria link the prize to ride-hailing activity, making the reward appear like compensation for services.

*Instead*=> Make eligibility conditional only on active participation in the branded advertising program, i.e. having the Bolt stickers on the car and submitting the monthly sticker photo.

 *Example*:

{quote}“All drivers who are part of the Branded Cars program and have submitted their November and December sticker verification photos are automatically entered into the prize draw.”{quote}

This keeps the reward clearly tied to the ad service, not driving volume, and is aligned with the current advertising contract structure (given that in fact, you expect 75% of drivers meeting this threshold).

# *Frame the lottery as a promotional campaign, not a reward for work*

Distinguish the lottery from a “bonus” and present it as a holiday promotional game for brand ambassadors.

Position the draw as a randomised giveaway for eligible participants, without implying performance or sales targets.

*Example*:

{quote}“As part of our festive campaign, we’re celebrating our most visible drivers with a holiday draw. Every eligible Branded Car is entered automatically – it’s our way of saying thank you for your help in promoting the Bolt brand!”{quote}

This aligns with how promotional giveaways are run by brands and avoids employment-like reward structures.

# *Include the legally required disclaimer visibly in all campaign materials*

*Example*:
On any digital banners, flyers, or in-app popups for the lottery:

{quote}“Cette campagne est destinée aux conducteurs participants à la publicité sur véhicule : Publicité pour la centrale de réservation Bolt.”{quote}

I asked where we are going to communicate, to understand the public exposure of the lotttery.

Happy to review the updated Terms & Conditions once drafted or help structure a version of the campaign text and visuals that stays on the safe side.

Hey [~accountid:712020:9cfda827-f644-48a1-9da8-aff3fd427bf9] !

On the idea of shortlisting fleets based on Bolt’s own criteria, we’d flag a few concerns from a legal and compliance standpoint:

* *Competition & fairness:* If Bolt selects which fleets appear on a public list, and this results in some fleets receiving more visibility or access to courier leads, it may be seen as favoring certain partners over others. This could raise concerns under competition law principles, especially if the selection criteria are not transparent or objectively applied.
* *Platform neutrality (P2B Regulation):* As a platform, we’re expected to treat business users (e.g. fleets) fairly and transparently. If we promote some but not others — without a clear, objective basis — it could be perceived as discriminatory or non-neutral.
* *Reputational risk:* Excluded fleets may raise fairness complaints, which could erode trust and potentially attract scrutiny if challenged.

To mitigate this, we’d suggest the following solution:

* send a communication re this *to all fleets*, asking for their *consent* and *asking for the Fleet to specify if they charge* onboarding fees or not.
* List *all Fleets who wishes so*, but then create a division on the ones who charge and the ones who do not charge:

For example:

_List of Fleets in Lisbon –> the couriers clicks -> 2 other titles appear that he can click on:_

_a) Fleets who charge onboarding fees_

* xxxxxx
* xxxxxx
* xxxxxx

_b) Fleets who do not charge onboarding fees._

* xxxxxx
* xxxxxx
* xxxxxx

In this case we are not excluding any Fleet, but we are informing beforehand the couriers which Fleets do not charge.

As for *lead tracking:* as mentioned earlier, Bolt should not collect or manage courier intent or contact tracking, as this reintroduces reclassification risks and blurs legal lines.

Thank you!

*Background*

*In short:*
* Who is writing: A lawyer representing Bolt driver Ibrahim Achati.
* What they want: The identity of the last driver registered in Bolt’s system for the same vehicle before the accident.
* Why: To pursue legal claims relating to a car accident.
* Bolt’s likely position: We cannot share such personal data unless required by law or by a competent authority (e.g. police, court).
Details:
* The lawyer represents Mr Ibrahim Achati, a Bolt driver in Germany, who was involved in a traffic accident on 30 October 2024.
* The purpose of the letter:
He’s asking Bolt to disclose which person last used or was registered as the driver of the vehicle (a Toyota Corolla, licence plate F-J 1631) on the Bolt platform before the date of the accident.
* In other words, the lawyer wants to know who was driving or logged into Bolt as a driver using that car before 30.10.2024 — likely to determine liability or insurance responsibility in the traffic case “Achati /. Belmonte” (the case number 010532-25 refers to that civil matter).
* This is essentially a request for identification of another driver, not a data subject rights request from the driver himself. It’s a third-party disclosure request for personal data, meaning Bolt cannot provide such information without a valid legal basis — for example, an official law enforcement or court order.
* Mr Achati is _not complaining about Bolt_, but is _using Bolt’s data ecosystem as a potential source of evidence_ in his private accident case against another party (“Belmonte”). He’s effectively asking Bolt to confirm *who last drove the car before the crash*, which Bolt cannot share unless compelled by *law enforcement or a court order*, since that would reveal *third-party personal data*.


*Relevance of the requested data*

Mr Achati says he received the car from his Bolt partner (fleet owner) — meaning he was not the vehicle owner, but drove it under a fleet arrangement.
After the accident, he is now apparently being held liable for damages (civilly or by insurance).
By asking who was last registered as the driver in Bolt’s system before him, his lawyer likely wants to:
* show that someone else had used the same vehicle earlier, possibly implying that this earlier driver could have caused existing damage or a mechanical issue;
* or argue that the car’s condition (tyres, brakes, etc.) had been compromised before Mr Achati used it, and therefore he should not be fully liable;
* or prove that another Bolt driver was still connected to that vehicle account close to the time of the crash — potentially to shift or share liability.
In short, the lawyer wants to trace who else drove the same car through Bolt before the accident, to see whether that person might be responsible for the vehicle’s state or for events leading to the crash.
However, the requested data (the identity of another driver) is not personal data of Mr Achati, and sharing it would disclose third-party personal data. So Bolt cannot release that information unless ordered by a court or competent authority — even if Mr Achati’s intention is legitimate from a legal defence perspective.

*LIA*

h3. 1. Overview of the request

*Authority:* Policía Foral de Navarra – Brigada de Delitos contra las Personas
*Type of request:* Urgent data disclosure for criminal investigation
*Case reference:* AT1993358
*Date:* 8 November 2025
*Purpose:* Investigation of a *serious assault* on a Bolt driver (grievous bodily harm)
*Data requested:*

* All data available in Bolt’s databases regarding a specific trip on *7 November 2025 (02:21–02:34)* in *Pamplona*, operated by driver _Iván de los Santos Bautista_ (Hyundai Ioniq5, reg. 5958NGT).
* Specifically: identifying data of the customer who ordered the ride (name, surname, DNI, phone number, email, address, etc.), in order to locate *two witnesses* of the assault.

*Legal basis cited:*
Article *22.3 of Organic Law 3/2018 (LOPDGDD)* on data protection.

----

h3. 2. Legal basis assessment

Article 22.3 LOPDGDD concerns *data retention for security camera footage* — it regulates the storage and provision of *video surveillance images*, not user data from digital platforms. It does *not* impose a general obligation on companies like Bolt to disclose user data to police.

Therefore, *the cited article is not a valid legal basis* for Bolt to share user data.

----

h3. 3. Scope and proportionality

The request is proportionate in scope (it targets a single ride) and justified (serious assault).
However, *a valid legal basis must still be established* before disclosing any data. Without it, Bolt cannot lawfully process or transfer the personal data under Article 6(1)(c) GDPR.

----

h3. 4. Recommendation

*→ Decline disclosure until a valid legal basis is provided.*

----

h3. 5. Summary for Jira

*Decision:* Decline
*Reason:* Invalid legal basis (Article 22.3 LOPDGDD – not applicable to Bolt).
*Next step:* CS to request clarification or a new request citing a valid article of the Criminal Procedure Act.
*Proportionality:* Acceptable once valid legal basis is provided.

Hi [~accountid:712020:a25cc8d9-692b-4200-aebf-19e86c575441],

In this case, campaign terms are not strictly necessary, as the initiative involves Bolt donating €1 per Bolt Electric trip directly from its own funds, without any financial contribution required from riders or drivers.

Since the donation comes entirely from Bolt and the campaign has a fixed cap of €10,000, it does not create any legal or contractual relationship with users that would require formal T&Cs.

That said, if marketing materials (e.g., app banners, emails, or social media posts) mention the campaign, it would be advisable to include *clear and simple disclosure language*, such as:

“Between November 26 and 28, Bolt will donate €1 from its own funds to Acción contra el Hambre for each Bolt Electric trip, up to a total of €10,000.”

This ensures transparency and avoids any misunderstanding by users regarding who is making the donation or whether their fare contributes to it.

As for the agreement with the NGO, it’s not strictly necessary, but we could optionally put in place a short MoU or simple donation agreement for clarity and documentation purposes.

I’d also recommend reviewing this [Confluence page on donations, |https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/MP/pages/4369187705/Donation+Categories+CSR+Partnerships#Which-Donation-Types-are-Authorised?]where you can find useful guidance and best practices. In addition, please coordinate with the Tax and Accounting teams to confirm any tax implications and to ensure the transfer of funds to the NGO is handled correctly -it will likely need to be made through the local entity.

Many thanks!

[~accountid:5d3b12432acc2d0c6219ff80] this is an incorrect impression. We don’t have any legal relationship with an OÜ just because a driver happens to hold a position there. In other words, *the mere fact that a driver is a board member of some OÜ does not create any relationship between Bolt and that OÜ, and therefore we cannot make any payouts to it.*

Each OÜ is a separate legal entity. If we were to send money to an OÜ, it would only be because we have a direct agreement with that OÜ. If a board member of an OÜ is also a driver on our platform and has accepted our T&Cs, then our relationship is with that driver personally. We can make payouts only to the driver directly — if they are registered as an FIE, then to their FIE bank account; and if they have an LHV account, then only to that account.

*Legal Basis – Taxi Act (Taxiloven)*
Under Danish law, specifically § 4(2) of the *Taxi Act (Taxiloven)*,
> _“Taxikørsel må kun sælges af et kørselskontor.”_
>  _(Taxi transport may only be sold by a dispatch centre.)_
This means that *only a licensed dispatch office (taxicentral)* can legally sell or market taxi or ride-hailing trips to passengers. Individual fleets, fleet owners (FOs), or drivers may operate vehicles, but they cannot sell the trip directly to the end customer.

As a result, *Bolt Rides DK ApS* holds the *dispatch-centre permit* and is therefore the legal seller of all rides dispatched through the Bolt platform in Denmark

*Contractual Basis – Agreement with Fleets*

The legal and commercial relationship confirming that *Bolt Rides DK ApS*, not the fleet, is the seller of services is established through two documents:
1. *[Platform Terms for Ride-Hailing Services: Service Providers (Denmark)|https://bolt.eu/en-dk/legal/platform-terms-for-ride-hailing-services-service-providers-denmark/?category=rides]*
2. *[Special Terms for Service Providers (Denmark)|https://bolt.eu/en-dk/legal/tnc-special-service-providers/]*
Together, these form the binding contractual framework between Bolt and all Danish fleets and FOs.

*1. Who sells the service*
 Section _“About Bolt and our relationship with you”_ of the Platform Terms states:
> “Bolt operates as a licensed taxi dispatch centre in Denmark. Bolt facilitates services by connecting Customers with Service Providers … and re-sells these services onwards to Customers (‘Ride-Hailing Services’).”
“Ride-Hailing Services” are further defined as:
> “Taxi transportation services which are provided to Customers by Bolt, fulfilled by Service Providers on behalf of Bolt, and arranged via the Bolt Platform.”
These clauses make it explicit that Bolt is the contractual seller to the Customer, while the fleet merely fulfills the service on Bolt’s behalf.

*2. How fleets are tied to Bolt’s dispatch authority*
 Clause 2.1 of the Special Terms for Service Providers (Denmark) requires that:
> “You shall be affiliated only with Bolt as a dispatch centre and shall not accept or fulfil taxi services via any other taxi dispatch centre in Denmark.”
Clause 5.4 clarifies that the fleet remains an independent contractor but operates under Bolt’s dispatch centre licence, not as its own seller.

*In summary*
The Platform Terms legally designate Bolt Rides DK ApS as the seller of services to riders.
The Special Terms require each fleet to affiliate exclusively with Bolt as its dispatch centre, confirming that they operate under Bolt’s licence and cannot sell rides independently.

Those two signed documents are the agreement that makes Bolt, not the fleet, the legal seller of ride-hailing services in Denmark.

Summary:

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
WorkSmart supplies a *contingent worker (temporary employee)* to Bolt under a German _Arbeitnehmerüberlassung (AÜG)_ agreement.
The individual will perform payroll administration for Bolt’s Germany and Switzerland markets, working directly within Bolt’s systems and under Bolt’s supervision.
{panel}

h3. *Assessment*

* *Nature of Processing:*
The worker, though employed by WorkSmart, operates under Bolt’s direction and accesses data only within Bolt’s controlled environment.
WorkSmart itself *does not process or control any Bolt employee data*.
* *Controller Relationship:*
Under GDPR, both parties act as *independent data controllers*:
** WorkSmart → controller for its own employees’ data.
** Bolt → controller for data processed within its own operations.
Therefore, there is *no controller–processor relationship* under Article 28 GDPR.
* *Conclusion:*
A *Data Processing Agreement (DPA) is not required*.
Instead, mutual data-protection and confidentiality obligations should be embedded within the main contract to ensure compliance and risk coverage.

{panel:bgColor=#e3fcef}
*Result:* following a few iterations, Worksmart and Bolt agreed on updated privacy clauses. The privacy clauses reflect the privacy obligations of WorkSmart as a _Arbeitnehmerüberlassung (AÜG)_ provider, who does not process Bolt’s personal data.
{panel}

If we want to keep a light activity condition, we can do it indirectly — for example:
“Eligible drivers are those who were active at least once during the campaign period and are part of the branded car program.” Would this work for you?
That keeps it minimal enough not to look like a performance target while still ensuring the driver base is engaged.

Switching from cash to a non-cash prize (like tech gear, vouchers, or branded rewards) also helps — it frames the campaign as a “brand giveaway” rather than an employment-linked bonus. A smaller cash value would reduce risk but wouldn’t change the underlying legal concern if activity thresholds remain.

Limiting comms to push notifications or in-app banners (not public website) is a good call — it keeps the campaign within the driver community and avoids public advertising scrutiny.

Happy to further discuss if needed.

This is now a recurring issue that’s becoming increasingly sensitive in the Malta market —  scheduled ride failures, particularly in the early morning hours and for airport transfers.

We’ve now received several complaints escalated via the MCCAA (Malta’s consumer regulator), most recently the one described in this ticket: a rider who scheduled a 4:00 AM trip to the airport, only to have the ride fail at the last minute with no alternative options available. 

My view is that, althought we are legally protected under our T&Cs (as no driver accepted and no contract of carriage was formed), the user expectation is that a scheduled ride is “guaranteed”, and the platform does little to counter that perception.

From a legal and consumer law standpoint, we’re still on solid ground, but:

* Repeated incidents are eroding user trust in the reliability of the platform.
* There’s growing risk of the MCCAA questioning whether the scheduled ride feature is misleading by omission, given how it’s currently presented in the app.
* These complaints are consuming increasing operational and legal bandwidth, and we risk reputational harm if this becomes a public narrative.

My view is that this needs to be treated not just as a complaint-by-complaint issue but as a broader product-policy risk. Even a small change — such as a clearer disclaimer in the app UI (e.g., “driver confirmation subject to availability”) or improved early-warning notifications — could significantly reduce frustration and liability exposure.

Suggest we consider:

* Minimal in-app copy changes (e.g. “confirmation subject to driver availability”);
* A review of how/when the feature is offered (especially during low-supply windows);
* Internal SOP alignment on messaging and goodwill handling.

_We hope this response clarifies our position and demonstrates our commitment to treating our customers with fairness and respect. Please do not hesitate to contact us should you require any further information._

_Yours sincerely,_

– The transaction will be treated under the *reverse charge mechanism*, so Bolt will self-account for VAT in Estonia.
– As Bolt will not issue an invoice, there will be *no additional VAT obligation for HNK*.

From an accounting perspective, since Bolt is providing a discount code rather than a prepaid voucher, the marketing expense will be *recognized progressively as rides are redeemed*, rather than upfront. Hi [~accountid:712020:3b323097-a7a7-4217-80f0-9db561b5900a] - thanks for raising this. 

Here are my brief replies, but I will defer to [~accountid:712020:8bcb68bd-f8da-4da1-8320-2536f6bb0c0c] for the final word on this from a tax perspective. 

# Yes, drivers should pay income tax on all income. Yes, show it as a separate line item. 
# Yes, show explicitly. Can it be labelled as “DPWRA Adjustment”? I think ‘other income’ is fine from a legal perspective. 
# In Canada, you should not exclude the entire order/time from the DPWRA calculation just because a refund was issued for driver fault. The time from acceptance → completion/cancellation is still “work-assignment” time and must count. Keep the order’s hours in, and handle misconduct separately via warnings/removal under the DPWRA process and our T&Cs. Please see the previous Q&A with Kyle on this: [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1azpEjfVvLS-ebRWJwzncXDp4tQ8r9taBtF2ZHNxWK8Y/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.tj4y8fl9gbze|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1azpEjfVvLS-ebRWJwzncXDp4tQ8r9taBtF2ZHNxWK8Y/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.tj4y8fl9gbze|smart-link]. Use net-of-refund earnings in the DPWRA math (i.e., subtract refunds). So in your example: fare CAD 10, refund CAD 4 → earnings = CAD 6 for DPWRA; the order’s hours stay in. DPWRA guarantees minimum wage for actual work-assignment time. If you excluded the order entirely (time + earnings), we risk an underpayment claim. 

Using net-of-refund earnings preserves DPWRA compliance while our T&Cs still let us adjust fares for violations and take action against repeat offenders (with reasons/notice).

* IMO *we should be asking for consent here via signatures / consent forms*. Although I appreciate that the event is small and that participants _might_ be fine with consenting verbally, we need to ensure that we have _recorded_ consents to use their images in marketing materials. People can get nervous when their likeness is used in advertising that they may not be aware of, and so to cover our bases we should make sure that we can evidence each participant’s consent if we need to. I have therefore adapted a consent form here ([LINK|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1mS6vDHNpypHwrsGVrInnYVOjSKj5q8J2Su769Ab7GBQ/edit?tab=t.0]), which we can use as a working draft. * On the question of whether we can collect multiple signatures in one table, rather than separate forms - This is a riskier approach, as (i) it could give the impression that we are bundling consents; and (ii) it may make it difficult to keep track of consents / withdrawal of consents from an operational POV. However, since the event is small and low risk, the *business can consider accepting this risk and proceed*, provided that we include a *separate notice at the event containing transparency information*. {color:#4c9aff}*Let me know if this raises any issues from a Romanian law POV*{color}.
** NB. We can further minimise the risk / strengthen the case for using a table to collect consents by ensuring that the photos are mostly wide shots.
* Finally, on the question of whether the instructor can use the photos to promote their own services, we could *include some additional language in the consent form* on this, as ideally we should collect the participants consent to share the photos given that they will be used for +_third-party_+ marketing as well. Hi team, 

Thank you for escalating! 
The customer has a negative balance due to a technical issue from Bolt’s end. 

This bug happens with Alternative Payment methods (APMs). APMs don’t have dual messaging — Authorization + Capture. They just have the capture. 
If the payment amount is lower than the captured amount then Bolt will automatically refund the difference. 

In this case the capture was for 16.12 PLN, but order price was just 10 PLN (cancellation fee). 
This triggered an automatic refund for 6.12 PLN. 

Now when the full refund for 10 PLN was issued then it triggered the bug/discrepancy between how the refund was recorded on the payment vs order. The full refund for payment was 16.12 PLN. However, for the order the full refund is 10 PLN. 

16.12 PLN - 10 PLN = 6.12 PLN. 

How to solve the issue for the customer? 
The customers balance cannot be amended. The only way we can solve the issue for the customer is to issue a Bolt Balance refund. 
Unfortunately, the customer payments team doesn’t have any accesses to issue refunds to to BB. 

Could you please issue a Bolt Balance refund for the customer for 6.12 PLN? You might not be able to issue the refund from the original order as the “refund has already been issued”. Could you please try to issue the refund from customers other recent orders? If you have any issues you might want to check with your team lead as they have higher permissions to refund from old orders. 

Please note that this has been escalated to payment engineers to fix here.

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Marten

# Analysis

I have analysed the articles mentioned, and in my opinion, they do not constitute a valid legal basis empowering the police with the right to request data from private entities such as Bolt. Instead, both *Articles 230 and 231* of the Code of Criminal Procedure merely define who qualifies as a _judicial police officer_ or _judicial policeman_, as well as their obligation to act under the direction of a public prosecutor when investigating an offence.

On the other hand, Articles 6 and 15 indeed specify exceptions to the general requirement of consent under the PDPA, however, they are not empowering the police officers with the right to collect/ request the data disclosure from private entities. 

*Opinion: These are not valid legal bases.*

A valid legal basis would be, in this case, for instance, Article 228 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which states:

{quote}_In conducting the investigation referred to in the preceding section a public prosecutor may set up a period of time and order the public prosecuting affairs official, judicial police officer specified in Article 230, or judicial policeman specified in Article 231 to investigate the circumstances of the offense,_ *_to collect evidence and to submit report thereof_*_; the case file and evidence may be delivered thereto at the same time if necessary._{quote}

# Further steps

Hi, [~accountid:712020:10daa261-d587-4bee-926d-af5c022abc8e] , my understanding is that the business decision is to proceed with signing this NDA as is. While I am not entirely opposed to this approach, given that negotiating the NDA would likely be a lengthy process, I would like to highlight the following red flags:

* *One-sided obligations:* NDA protects only Purem; the Business Partner(Bolt)’s information is not covered.
* *Very broad definition of confidential information:* includes all types of data, even oral or implied information, without requiring written marking.
* *Strict information-security and audit requirements:* references Purem’s own standards (TISAX®/ISO 27001) and allows Purem to audit compliance at any time.
* *No liability for Purem:* it disclaims responsibility for accuracy or completeness of shared information.
* *Unlimited indemnity:* the Business Partner is fully liable for any breach, including those of affiliates or subcontractors.
* *Extended duration:* obligations last *10 years* and continue indefinitely until data becomes public.
* *Governing law:* *German law* applies and disputes are settled by *ICC arbitration in Zurich* – *we usually do not accept this*, as Bolt’s policy limits governing law to *Estonian or Romanian law*.

Given that the NDA is heavily favorable to Purem, it is up to you  to decide whether to:

* *Proceed as is*, accepting the German-law framework and one-sided terms; or
* *Enter a longer review and negotiation process* involving Purem’s legal department in Germany to align terms (especially governing law and reciprocity).

Thank you!

Hi [~accountid:712020:632a94a1-c879-41ac-8205-40429df7b583] ,

Under Portuguese law, meal cards (cartões de refeição) may be used for the purchase of meals or food products, either in establishments where they are prepared and consumed or in take-away and delivery formats.

That said, there are a few important topics that need to be addressed before anything else:

* First, in my POV, the Agency Fee (our delivery service fee) cannot be paid using a meal card, since it does not qualify as an eligible expense under the applicable regulations. Meal cards are strictly limited to the purchase of food, so delivery charges, tips, promotions or other services (like Bolt’s intermediary fee) fall outside of scope. This would require a technical solution that prevents the use of meal cards to cover that part of the order.
* Second, as you flagged, we might have a legal entity issue here: If Bolt Food operates under the same NIF as Bolt RH — and Bolt RH is not legally categorized as a food merchant or meal provider — then accepting meal cards under this NIF could violate the applicable regulations.
Even if the food is provided by restaurant partners, Bolt would still be the payment intermediary, and this could expose Bolt to liability if the card is used outside the permitted scope.

Finally, from an operational standpoint, this would not be straightforward to implement:
- We would likely need separate onboarding and validation for each restaurant, since most issuers only authorize payment to pre-approved merchants;
- We’d also need technical mechanisms to prevent misuse.

*LLM Validation (Base Layer)*

* *Vendor*: Upstash Inc., Delaware-registered (U.S.) operator of [upstash.com|http://upstash.com] and [upstash.io|http://upstash.io] 
* *Product Type*: Context-injection service using the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Not an LLM or agent.
* *Jurisdiction*: U.S./EU hosting;
* *Infrastructure & Compliance:*
** SOC 2 and SSO for Enterprise plan
* *Data Usage*
** Queries processed locally; only derived “topics” sent to Upstash servers.
** *Security Issue found during screening*: private-repo scanner indexed entire repositories instead of configured folders, potentially exposing unintended files ([Github issue|https://github.com/upstash/context7/issues/1020])
** [Context7 is community driven|https://github.com/upstash/context7/blob/master/README.md#%EF%B8%8F-disclaimer]
*** _Context7 projects are community-contributed and while we strive to maintain high quality, we cannot guarantee the accuracy, completeness, or security of all library documentation. …  By using Context7, you acknowledge that you do so at your own discretion and risk._



 *Capability Assessment (Functional Layer)* 

Context7 acts as an MCP provider, not a generative agent. It provides accurate, version-specific documentation and metadata to LLMs (such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Cursor) to enhance output reliability.

* *How Context7 MCP Works* 
** Users install the MCP client (e.g., for Cursor, Claude Code, VS Code) and configure an MCP server pointing at Context7. 
** The prompt syntax: when a developer writes something like: “How do I invalidate a query in React Query? use context7”, the MCP client automatically triggers the Context7 tools.
** Two main tools exposed via the MCP protocol:
*** resolve-library-id — input: libraryName (string). Returns one or more “Context7-compatible library IDs” (for example /vercel/next.js, /mongodb/docs).
*** get-library-docs — input: context7CompatibleLibraryID (string), optional topic (string, e.g., “routing”), optional tokens (number, default 5000, but min enforced 1000). Returns formatted documentation text for injection.
** Internally the docs pipeline works like this:
*** Search for docs based on the library name.
*** Fetch and preprocess documentation (extract code snippets, explanations).  ￼
*** Format and inject the documentation into the prompt context the LLM uses. 
* *Private Repository Support*
** Admins can add private repositories as documentation sources for Context7.
** Once added, these repos are indexed and treated as internal libraries accessible via resolve-library-id and get-library-docs.
* *Processing Pipeline*
** Context7 locates the relevant documentation, extracts structured text and snippets, performs preprocessing (e.g., deduplication, formatting), and returns only the relevant context within the defined token limit.

*Editor Compatibility (Integration Layer)*

Context7 supports a wide range of MCP-enabled environments including:

* Cursor: configuration via ~/.cursor/mcp.json or a one-click button in Settings.  ￼
* Claude Code: supports remote or local server configuration for Context7.  ￼
* Visual Studio Code: configuration by adding the “context7” MCP server in settings.json with HTTP or stdio transport.  ￼
* JetBrains AI Assistant: MCP server can be added via Settings → Tools → AI Assistant → Model Context Protocol (MCP) with JSON configuration.  ￼
* Other client environments: e.g., Zed, Cline, Amp, Perplexity, etc. Each supports standard MCP configuration for Context7.  ￼

*Additional Capabilities (Differentiation Layer)*

* Core: Live, version-aware documentation injection.
* Extensibility: context7.json for internal libs/private repos.
* Self-Hosting: Context7 Local for data isolation.
* Transparency: Open-source MCP server.
* Limitation: Relies on external LLMs.

*Token Usage & Cost Impact*

When users use context7 to get docs.

||*Context Size*||*Total Tokens / Query*||*Relative Cost*||*Added Cost (GPT-4o)*||
|None|≈ 200|1×|–|
|+1 000 docs|≈ 1 200|6×|+$0.006|
|+3 000 docs|≈ 3 200|16×|+$0.016|
|+5 000 docs|≈ 5 200|25×|+$0.025|

Use topic and tokens parameters to limit context size and control cost.

*Cost and Licensing*

[Pricing Tiers |http://context7.com/docs/plans-pricing￼]

||*Plan*||*Monthly Cost (per seat)*||*Notes*||
|*Free*|$0|Access to public libraries only|
|*Pro*|$7 / seat / month
$15 per 1 M tokens of parsed content
Note: e.g. MongoDb has 15.8M tokens|Private repo|
|*Enterprise*|same as pro or better|* SOC-2
* SSO|

*Example Monthly Estimate*

Assuming 4 engineers on Pro plan + 500 k tokens of private-repo content:

* Seats: 4 × $7  = $28 / month

* Private-repo indexing: 0.5 M × ($15 / 1 M) = $7.50 / month

* ≈ $35.50 total excluding LLM API costs.



h2. Overall Decision: REJECT

Why:

*  Private-repo scanner vulnerability: Known issue (#1020￼) caused Context7 to index entire repositories instead of only specified folders, risk of overexposure for internal code.
* Their disclaimer about [community driven|https://github.com/upstash/context7/blob/master/README.md#%EF%B8%8F-disclaimer].
* Token-usage overhead: Injecting documentation increases LLM token consumption and API costs (up to 20–25× per long query).
* From the documentation it appears that when you add a private repository for docs in Context7, the repo must contain documentation files (e.g. .md files) or folders you explicitly include.

Hello [~accountid:712020:13cbe2f1-9fb3-4612-8eaf-1fdee09b633f], 

The payments have been successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

 Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Afiba

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Marten

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

* No clear impact observed in the first 3 weeks due to the noise from Halloween (1 Nov) + BNP tests (28th Oct - 4th Nov).
* Comparing the first 2 weeks of Oct vs Nov:
** *ASP:* −5% (vs −5% expected)
** *S2O:* +2% / +0.9pp (increases strongest in short & long trips)
** *O2F:* −0.4% / −0.3pp (*affirms that market can take sharp price drops without hurting supply*)
* Sessions +16% in Nov → FR & GMV uplift largely driven by organic demand, not pricing.
** *FR:* +17% (vs +9% expected)
** *GMV:* +11% (vs +3% expected)
** _Seasonality:_ Last year Nov saw declines (FR/GMV −10% MoM). This year we’re up +17% FR and +11% GMV, but price-change contribution is not quantifiable
* Market Share: +2pp MS vs early Oct (seen in both Fox & Visa), not attributed to price change but we have maintained the MS growth in the recent weeks.
** Oct MS improvement was mostly from long bins, Nov data will tell us how this price drop worked out for MS across bins.
* Pricing vs Competition in the last 2 weeks: we appear 1–5% more expensive than Uber due to RVP, but distance-level analysis shows we’re cheaper for most distances.

Next steps:

# Uber likely uses dynamic/peak-hour pricing, so small-sample window-shopping comparisons may mislead. *No base-price changes recommended for now.*
# We'll proceed with pricing review of the next granularity: *Category wise optimization*
## Our utilization is still only 50%. To keep our supply engaged enough and minimize any risk of losing them to competition, we should work towards 60% which can only be achieved with further price drops
## We have only achieved 2% improvement in S2O (vs target 5%) and still fail to convert 50% of incoming sessions.
